subject: sci
title: Physics: Motion, Forces, Newton's Laws, Work, Simple Machines, and Momentum
objectives: You will calculate speed, velocity, and acceleration and explain the difference between speed and velocity.
You will read distance-time and speed-time graphs to describe an object's motion and calculate speed or acceleration from them.
You will find the net force on an object, apply Newton's three laws of motion, and use F = ma.
You will calculate work (W = Fd) and power (P = W/t) and explain how simple machines provide mechanical advantage.
You will calculate momentum (p = mv) and use conservation of momentum to predict the result of a simple collision.

slides.title: Physics: Motion, Forces, Work, and Momentum
slides.board:
Today you will:

  • Calculate speed, velocity, and acceleration
  • Read distance-time and speed-time graphs
  • Find net force and use Newton's three laws and F = ma
  • Calculate work and power; explain simple machines
  • Calculate momentum and solve a simple collision

Plan: Warm-up → 8 big ideas → practice together → your turn → GED-style questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 8 of Science: physics. Physical science is about 40 percent of the GED Science test, and motion and forces show up again and again. The good news is that this topic runs on a handful of short formulas, and the GED almost always gives you the formula in the question. Your job is to pick the right numbers, keep the units straight, and know what a graph is telling you. That is exactly what we practice today.
ask: When you are in a car and the driver brakes hard, which way does your body lurch? (expected answer: forward; hold onto that, it is Newton's first law and we will explain it today)

slides.title: Warm-Up: Chemistry Review
slides.board:
1. An atom has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. How many neutrons does it have?
  2. A rock has a mass of 60 g and a volume of 20 mL. What is its density?
  3. Balance: __H2 + __O2 → __H2O
  4. Ice melting into water: physical change or chemical change?
  5. A cleaner has a pH of 11. Is it an acid or a base?
steps: 1. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12.
2. Density = mass ÷ volume = 60 g ÷ 20 mL = 3 g/mL.
3. 2H2 + 1O2 → 2H2O. Check: 4 H and 2 O on each side.
4. Physical. It is still water (H2O); only the state changed.
5. Base. A pH above 7 is basic.

notes.say: These five come from last week's chemistry lesson. Give yourself about three minutes, then tell me each answer before I reveal it. Pay special attention to number 2: density is a formula with a division and units, and today every formula works the same way. Write the formula, plug in the numbers with their units, then calculate.
ask: What does the mass number count? (expected answer: protons plus neutrons)
Why can't you change the subscript in H<sub>2</sub>O to balance the equation? (expected answer: that would make a different substance; change only coefficients)
notes.answer: 1. 12 neutrons. 2. 3 g/mL. 3. 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. 4. Physical change. 5. Base.
notes.watch: On number 2, some students multiply (1,200) instead of dividing. Ask them to say the formula out loud first: density equals mass divided by volume. The same habit fixes most errors today.

slides.title: Big Idea 1: Speed and Velocity
slides.board:
speed = distance ÷ time   (s = d ÷ t)

NeedUse
speeds = d ÷ t
distanced = s × t
timet = d ÷ s

Units: a distance per a time (m/s, km/h, mi/h).

Velocity = speed plus a direction: 20 m/s north.

notes.say: Speed answers one question: how fast? You divide the distance by the time, and the unit tells you the recipe: meters per second means meters divided by seconds. The same formula can be turned around to find distance or time. Velocity is speed with a direction attached. Two cars both going 50 miles per hour, one north and one south, have the same speed but different velocities.
ask: A car drives around a curve at a steady 30 mi/h. Is its velocity changing? (expected answer: yes; the speed stays the same, but the direction changes)
If you go 100 m in 20 s, what is your speed? (expected answer: 5 m/s)
notes.watch: Students often divide time by distance. Point to the unit: miles per hour puts miles on top. The thing after "per" goes on the bottom.

slides.title: Worked Example: Speed with a Unit Change
slides.board: A bus travels 45 km in 30 minutes. What is its average speed in km/h?
steps: Formula: s = d ÷ t. The answer must be in km per hour, so time must be in hours.
Convert: 30 min ÷ 60 = 0.5 h.
Calculate: 45 km ÷ 0.5 h = 90 km/h.
Check: half an hour gives 45 km, so a full hour would give twice that, 90 km. Reasonable.

notes.say: Watch the units before the arithmetic. The question asks for kilometers per hour, but the time is in minutes, so I convert first: 60 minutes is one hour, so 30 minutes is half an hour. Then I divide. Finally I ask whether the answer makes sense, and doubling half an hour's distance confirms it.
ask: What answer do you get if you skip the conversion? (expected answer: 45 ÷ 30 = 1.5, which is km per minute, not km/h)
notes.watch: The answer 1.5 is the classic trap. It is a real number, just in the wrong unit (km/min). Always match the time unit to the unit in the question.

slides.title: Big Idea 2: Acceleration
slides.board:
a = (final speed − starting speed) ÷ time

Unit: m/s2 ("meters per second, every second").

Speeding upSlowing downTurning
positive anegative adirection changes

All three are acceleration, because velocity changes.

notes.say: Acceleration measures how fast the velocity changes. Take the change in speed, final minus starting, and divide by the time it took. If a car goes from 0 to 20 meters per second in 5 seconds, its speed climbs 4 meters per second every second, so its acceleration is 4 m/s squared. Slowing down gives a negative number, and turning at a steady speed is also acceleration, because the direction part of velocity changes.
ask: A car moves at a steady 25 m/s on a straight road. What is its acceleration? (expected answer: 0; the speed is not changing)
notes.watch: Students subtract in the wrong order and lose the sign. Insist on final minus starting, every time.

slides.title: Worked Example: Slowing Down
slides.board: A cyclist slows from 12 m/s to 4 m/s in 4 s. What is her acceleration?
steps: Formula: a = (final − starting) ÷ time.
Plug in: a = (4 m/s − 12 m/s) ÷ 4 s.
Subtract, then divide: −8 ÷ 4 = −2 m/s2.
Meaning: the negative sign tells us she is slowing down, losing 2 m/s of speed each second (12 → 10 → 8 → 6 → 4).

notes.say: Same formula, but now the final speed is smaller than the starting speed, so the change is negative. A negative acceleration in a straight line means slowing down. I like to check by counting: lose 2 every second for 4 seconds, and 12 drops to 4. It works.
ask: How would a GED question describe this without a minus sign? (expected answer: 'decelerating at 2 m/s<sup>2</sup>' or 'slowing down by 2 m/s each second')

slides.title: Big Idea 3: Motion Graphs
slides.board:
Read the y-axis label first!

Line shapeDistance-timeSpeed-time
Flatstoppedconstant speed
Slopes upmoving at constant speed (steeper = faster)speeding up
Slopes downmoving back toward startslowing down

Distance-time slope = speed. Speed-time slope = acceleration.

notes.say: This table is the most important thing on the board today, because the GED loves motion graphs and the two kinds look alike. A flat line means stopped on a distance-time graph, because the distance is not changing. The same flat line on a speed-time graph means the speed is not changing, so the object is cruising at a steady speed. The slope, rise over run, gives you speed on the first kind and acceleration on the second.
ask: A speed-time graph shows a flat line at 0. What is the object doing? (expected answer: it is stopped; its speed is zero)
On a distance-time graph, which is faster: a steep line or a gentle line? (expected answer: steep; more distance in the same time)
notes.watch: The number one error this week: calling a flat speed-time line "stopped." Make students say the y-axis label out loud before every graph question.

slides.title: Worked Example: Reading a Distance-Time Graph
slides.board:
Maya walks from home to a store, stopping to talk with a neighbor on the way.

(a) When was she stopped? (b) What was her speed from 0 to 10 min? (c) When was she fastest?
steps: Check the axes: y is distance, so this is a distance-time graph.
(a) The line is flat at 800 m from 10 to 20 minutes. Distance not changing = stopped.
(b) 0–10 min: 800 m ÷ 10 min = 80 m/min.
(c) 20–30 min: (2,000 − 800) m ÷ 10 min = 120 m/min. That is faster than 80 m/min, and the line is steeper there.
Bonus: average speed for the whole trip = 2,000 m ÷ 30 min ≈ 66.7 m/min (the stop counts).

notes.say: First I read the axes, every time. Then I look for flat parts, because on a distance-time graph flat means stopped. For each moving part, I divide the change in distance by the change in time. The steeper line gives the bigger number, so the picture and the arithmetic agree.
ask: Why is the average speed for the trip lower than both moving speeds? (expected answer: the 10-minute stop is part of the total time)
notes.watch: For part (c), some students divide 2,000 by 30 using the final reading instead of the change. Remind them: speed for a piece of the trip uses the change in distance over that piece.

slides.title: We Do: Reading a Speed-Time Graph
slides.board:
A city bus pulls away from a stop, drives, then stops at the next corner.

  1. What is the bus's acceleration from 0 to 6 s?
  2. Describe its motion from 6 to 8 s.
  3. What is its acceleration from 8 to 12 s?
  4. The bus has a mass of 10,000 kg. Preview: what net force acts on it from 0 to 6 s? (F = m × a)
steps: Check the axes: y is speed, so this is a speed-time graph.
1. a = (12 − 0) ÷ 6 = 2 m/s2 (speeding up).
2. Flat at 12 m/s: constant speed of 12 m/s, acceleration 0. Not stopped!
3. a = (0 − 12) ÷ (12 − 8) = −12 ÷ 4 = −3 m/s2 (slowing down).
4. F = 10,000 kg × 2 m/s2 = 20,000 N.

notes.say: Let's do this one together. You read the graph and tell me the numbers; I will write them into the formula. Start with the axis label, then work one piece of the graph at a time. Number 4 previews the next big idea: once you know the acceleration and the mass, Newton's second law gives you the force.
ask: What would the line look like if the bus were parked? (expected answer: flat along the x-axis at 0 m/s)
Which piece has the steeper slope, 0–6 s or 8–12 s? (expected answer: 8–12 s; it changes 12 m/s in only 4 s)
notes.answer: 1. 2 m/s2. 2. Constant speed, 12 m/s (acceleration 0). 3. −3 m/s2 (slowing by 3 m/s each second). 4. 20,000 N.
notes.watch: For question 3, students often divide by 12 (the clock reading) instead of 4 (the time the slowdown took). The time in the formula is the length of the interval.

slides.title: Big Idea 4: Forces and Net Force
slides.board:
A force is a push or pull, measured in newtons (N).

  • Same direction: add.
  • Opposite directions: subtract; the net force points toward the larger one.
Net force = 0Net force ≠ 0
balanced: no change in motionunbalanced: object accelerates

Weight is a force: weight = m × g, g ≈ 9.8 m/s2.

notes.say: Almost every object has several forces on it at once: gravity, a push, friction, air resistance. What matters is the net force, the total after you combine them. Draw an arrow for each force. Arrows pointing the same way add; arrows pointing opposite ways subtract. If everything cancels, the forces are balanced and the motion does not change. That means a resting object stays at rest, and a moving object keeps cruising at the same speed in the same direction.
ask: A book sits on a table. Gravity pulls it down. Why doesn't it fall? (expected answer: the table pushes up with an equal force, so the net force is zero)
What is the weight of a 10-kg bag? (expected answer: 10 × 9.8 = 98 N)
notes.watch: Students think balanced forces mean the object must be still. A car on cruise control on a straight, level road also has balanced forces. Balanced means no change in motion.

slides.title: Worked Example: Net Force and Acceleration
slides.board: A 50-kg sled sits on snow. Ana pulls it to the right with 180 N. Ben also pulls to the right with 70 N. Friction acts to the left with 50 N. Find the net force and the sled's acceleration.
steps: Same direction (right): 180 N + 70 N = 250 N right.
Opposite direction (left): 250 N − 50 N = 200 N to the right.
Second law: a = F ÷ m = 200 N ÷ 50 kg = 4 m/s2 to the right.
Unit check: N ÷ kg = m/s<sup>2</sup>, because 1 N = 1 kg·m/s<sup>2</sup>.

notes.say: I combine the arrows first: the two pulls to the right add, then friction to the left subtracts. Only after I have the net force do I use F equals m a. A very common mistake is to plug just one force, like Ana's 180 newtons, into the formula. The F in F equals m a is always the net force.
ask: What acceleration would you get if you forgot friction? (expected answer: 250 ÷ 50 = 5 m/s<sup>2</sup>, which is too big)

slides.title: Big Idea 5: Newton's Three Laws
slides.board:
LawBig ideaExample
1st (inertia)No net force → no change in motionBus brakes; riders lurch forward
2nd (F = ma)More force → more acceleration; more mass → less accelerationEmpty cart speeds up more than a full one
3rd (action-reaction)Forces come in equal, opposite pairs on two different objectsSwimmer pushes wall back; wall pushes swimmer forward

notes.say: Newton's first law is about inertia: objects keep doing what they were doing unless an unbalanced force acts. Your body keeps moving forward when the bus stops, because nothing stopped you yet. The second law puts numbers on it: F equals m times a, so you can solve for any one of the three. The third law says forces come in pairs: if you push on something, it pushes back on you just as hard, in the opposite direction. Those two forces act on different objects, so they never cancel each other out.
ask: Why does a full shopping cart take more effort to start than an empty one? (expected answer: more mass means more inertia; by the second law, the same force gives less acceleration)
A rocket has nothing to push against in space. How does it move? (expected answer: it pushes exhaust gas backward, and the gas pushes the rocket forward: third law)
notes.watch: "If the forces are equal and opposite, why does anything move?" Answer: third-law pairs act on different objects. To find whether one object accelerates, add only the forces acting on that object.

slides.title: We Do: Which Law Is It?
slides.board:
Name the law of motion each example shows best.

  1. A magician yanks a tablecloth fast, and the dishes stay in place.
  2. The same kick sends a soccer ball much faster than a bowling ball.
  3. A man steps off a small rowboat onto a dock, and the boat drifts backward.
  4. A car on cruise control moves at a steady 55 mi/h on a straight, level road. What is the net force on it?
steps: 1. First law. The dishes were at rest and tend to stay at rest; the quick pull gives little time for friction to move them.
2. Second law. Same force, less mass, so more acceleration (a = F ÷ m).
3. Third law. He pushes the boat backward; the boat pushes him forward.
4. Zero. Steady speed in a straight line means no acceleration, so the forces are balanced (first law). The engine's push equals friction plus air resistance.

notes.say: Use three key words. If something keeps doing what it was doing, think first law, inertia. If the example compares force, mass, and how fast things speed up, think second law. If two objects push on each other, think third law. You tell me which law, and why, before I reveal it.
ask: In number 3, which two objects are the force pair? (expected answer: the man and the boat)
notes.answer: 1. First law. 2. Second law. 3. Third law. 4. Net force = 0 (balanced forces; first law).
notes.watch: For number 4, many students say the engine force is bigger "because the car is moving." Motion does not need a net force; only a change in motion does.

slides.title: You Do: Motion and Force
slides.board:
Work alone. You have 4 minutes.

  1. A train travels 240 km in 3 h. What is its average speed?
  2. A car speeds up from 10 m/s to 25 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration?
  3. A box is pushed 90 N to the right while friction pulls 30 N to the left. What is the net force?
  4. What net force gives a 1,500-kg car an acceleration of 2 m/s2?
steps: 1. 240 ÷ 3 = 80 km/h
2. (25 − 10) ÷ 5 = 15 ÷ 5 = 3 m/s2
3. 90 − 30 = 60 N to the right
4. 1,500 × 2 = 3,000 N

notes.say: Your turn. Write the formula first for each one, then plug in. I am watching the clock, not your screen, so tell me when you are done and read me your answers with units. Units count: an answer without a unit is only half an answer.
ask: Read me your answers with units. (expected answer: 80 km/h; 3 m/s<sup>2</sup>; 60 N right; 3,000 N)
notes.answer: 1. 80 km/h. 2. 3 m/s2. 3. 60 N to the right. 4. 3,000 N.
notes.watch: On number 2, listen for 5 m/s2 (25 ÷ 5, forgetting the starting speed) or 7 m/s2 (35 ÷ 5, adding the speeds). Ask: "How much did the speed change?"

slides.title: Big Idea 6: Work and Power
slides.board:
Work: W = F × d   joules (J)
Power: P = W ÷ t   watts (W)

Work happens only when a force moves an object in the direction of the force.

Work doneNo work done
Lifting a box onto a shelfHolding a box still
Pushing a cart across a lotPushing a wall that does not move

notes.say: In everyday talk, holding a heavy box for a minute is hard work. In physics it is zero work, because the box does not move. Work is force times the distance the object moves in the direction of the force, and the unit is the joule. Power is how fast you do the work: the same job done in half the time takes twice the power. Watch the letters: W stands for work in the formula, but W is also the symbol for watts.
ask: Two people carry identical boxes up the same stairs. One runs, one walks. Who does more work? Who uses more power? (expected answer: same work; the runner uses more power)
notes.watch: Students multiply by time when finding power. Power is work divided by time: faster work, smaller time, bigger power.

slides.title: Worked Example: Work and Power
slides.board:
Carlos pushes a loaded cart with a steady 150 N force for 20 m across a parking lot. It takes 10 s.

(a) How much work does he do? (b) What is his power? (c) He then holds a 200-N box still for 30 s. How much work does he do on the box?
steps: (a) W = F × d = 150 N × 20 m = 3,000 J.
(b) P = W ÷ t = 3,000 J ÷ 10 s = 300 W.
(c) The box does not move, so d = 0 and W = 200 N × 0 m = 0 J.
Notice: time is not part of work. It only matters for power.

notes.say: Work first, then power, always in that order, because power needs the work. In part c, notice that time does not appear in the work formula at all. Holding still for thirty seconds or thirty minutes, the distance is zero, so the work is zero.
ask: If Carlos pushed the same cart the same distance in 5 s, what would change? (expected answer: work stays 3,000 J; power doubles to 600 W)

slides.title: Big Idea 7: Simple Machines
slides.board:
Six simple machines: lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane (ramp), wedge, screw.

A machine does not reduce work. It trades less force for more distance.

MA = output force ÷ input force

  • Ramp: MA = length ÷ height
  • Lever: MA = effort arm ÷ load arm
  • Fixed pulley: MA = 1 (changes direction); movable pulley: MA = 2

notes.say: A simple machine is a trade. You push with less force, but you push over a longer distance, so force times distance, the work, stays the same in an ideal machine. Real machines have friction, so you actually do a bit more work, never less. Mechanical advantage tells you how many times the machine multiplies your force. A ramp four times as long as it is high lets you push with one-fourth of the weight.
ask: Why does a long, gentle ramp take less force than a short, steep one to the same height? (expected answer: the same work is spread over a longer distance, so the force is smaller)
notes.watch: The myth to kill: "machines save work." Repeat the phrase: less force, more distance, same work.

slides.title: Worked Example: Moving a Piano Up a Ramp
slides.board: A 900-N piano must be raised 1.5 m onto a stage using a 6-m ramp. Ignoring friction, what force is needed along the ramp? What is the ramp's mechanical advantage?

figure.alt: A ramp drawn as a right triangle. The sloped side is labeled ramp length 6 m. The vertical side is labeled height 1.5 m. An arrow along the slope is labeled push 225 N.

steps: Work to lift straight up: W = 900 N × 1.5 m = 1,350 J.
Ideal ramp: same work along the ramp: F × 6 m = 1,350 J.
F = 1,350 J ÷ 6 m = 225 N.
MA = output force ÷ input force = 900 N ÷ 225 N = 4. Check: length ÷ height = 6 ÷ 1.5 = 4.

notes.say: The work method always works: find the work to lift the load straight up, then spread that same work over the length of the ramp. The movers push with only 225 newtons instead of 900, but they push it 6 meters instead of 1.5. The two ways of finding mechanical advantage agree, which is a great self-check.
ask: What force would a 3-m ramp to the same stage need? (expected answer: 1,350 ÷ 3 = 450 N; MA = 2)

slides.title: We Do: Levers and Pulleys
slides.board:
1. A worker uses a steel bar as a lever to lift a 600-N rock. The rock is 1 m from the fulcrum; she pushes 3 m from the fulcrum. What is the ideal MA? What effort force does she need?
  2. To lift the rock 0.2 m, how far down must she push her end?
  3. A single movable pulley lifts a 400-N load. What is the ideal effort force?

figure.alt: A lever: a straight bar resting on a triangular fulcrum. A 600-N rock sits on the short end, 1 m from the fulcrum. The effort pushes down on the long end, 3 m from the fulcrum.
figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 380 190' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><line x1='30' y1='100' x2='330' y2='100' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='5'/><polygon points='93,130 117,130 105,103' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='30' y='62' width='44' height='36' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='22' y='52' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>rock 600 N</text><line x1='330' y1='40' x2='330' y2='94' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='3'/><polygon points='330,98 324,86 336,86' fill='#0A1F3D' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><text x='290' y='30' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>effort</text><line x1='30' y1='160' x2='105' y2='160' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><text x='30' y='180' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>load arm 1 m</text><line x1='105' y1='160' x2='330' y2='160' stroke='#0A1F3D'/><text x='180' y='180' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>effort arm 3 m</text><text x='122' y='128' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D'>fulcrum</text></svg>

steps: 1. MA = effort arm ÷ load arm = 3 m ÷ 1 m = 3. Effort = 600 N ÷ 3 = 200 N.
2. Her end moves 3 times as far: 0.2 m × 3 = 0.6 m. Check work: 600 N × 0.2 m = 120 J = 200 N × 0.6 m.
3. A movable pulley has MA = 2: 400 N ÷ 2 = 200 N (she pulls 2 m of rope for every 1 m the load rises).

notes.say: Together now. For the lever, the long side is where she pushes, so the effort arm is 3 meters. Divide the arms to get the mechanical advantage, then divide the load by it to get the effort. Number 2 shows the trade in action: she gets a third of the force but moves three times as far, and the work matches on both ends.
ask: Where should she put the fulcrum to make the job even easier? (expected answer: closer to the rock, to make the load arm shorter and the effort arm longer)
notes.watch: Students flip the arms (1 ÷ 3) and get an MA less than 1, then multiply the load. Remind them: a helpful lever has MA greater than 1, so the effort is smaller than the load.

slides.title: Big Idea 8: Momentum
slides.board:
Momentum: p = m × v   (kg·m/s)

Objectm × vp
0.2-kg ball at 30 m/s0.2 × 306
3-kg ball at 2 m/s3 × 26
parked truckm × 00

Conservation: with no outside force, total momentum before a collision = total momentum after.

notes.say: Momentum is mass in motion: mass times velocity. It explains why a slow loaded truck is harder to stop than a fast baseball. Look at the table: a light, fast ball and a heavy, slow ball can have exactly the same momentum, and anything parked has none at all. In a collision, momentum is not lost; it is shared. Add up the momentum before, and the total after is the same.
ask: Which is harder to stop: a 2,000-kg truck at 1 m/s or a 0.15-kg baseball at 40 m/s? (expected answer: the truck; 2,000 vs. 6 kg·m/s)
notes.watch: Students compare only speed or only mass. Momentum needs both: multiply every time.

slides.title: Worked Example: A Collision
slides.board: A 1,500-kg car moving at 10 m/s rear-ends a 1,000-kg car that is stopped. The cars lock together. How fast do they move just after the collision?
steps: Momentum before: (1,500 × 10) + (1,000 × 0) = 15,000 kg·m/s.
Momentum after = momentum before = 15,000 kg·m/s.
Mass after (stuck together): 1,500 + 1,000 = 2,500 kg.
v = p ÷ m = 15,000 ÷ 2,500 = 6 m/s.

notes.say: Three moves: total momentum before, set it equal to total momentum after, then divide by the combined mass. The speed drops from 10 to 6 because the same momentum is now shared by more mass. If you ever get an answer faster than the moving car's starting speed, something went wrong.
ask: What speed would you get if you forgot to add the second car's mass? (expected answer: 15,000 ÷ 1,500 = 10 m/s, as if nothing happened)

slides.title: You Do: Work, Power, and Machines
slides.board:
Work alone. You have 4 minutes.

  1. You lift an 80-N box 1.5 m onto a shelf. How much work do you do?
  2. The lift took 4 s. What was your power?
  3. A 500-N barrel is rolled up a 5-m ramp onto a platform 1 m high. Ignoring friction, what force is needed along the ramp, and what is the MA?
steps: 1. W = 80 × 1.5 = 120 J
2. P = 120 ÷ 4 = 30 W
3. Work = 500 × 1 = 500 J; F = 500 ÷ 5 = 100 N; MA = 500 ÷ 100 = 5 (check: 5 m ÷ 1 m)

notes.say: Your turn again. Same routine: formula, numbers with units, calculate, check. When you finish, tell me your three answers and one sentence about why the ramp does not save work.
ask: Why doesn't the ramp save work? (expected answer: the force is smaller, but you push 5 m instead of 1 m; 100 N × 5 m = 500 J, the same work)
notes.watch: Listen for 480 W on number 2 (multiplying 120 by 4). Ask: "Does a faster lift mean more power or less?" Then: "So should time be on the bottom or the top?"

slides.title: You Do: Momentum
slides.board:
Work alone. You have 4 minutes.

  1. What is the momentum of a 0.5-kg ball moving at 12 m/s?
  2. Which has more momentum: a 70-kg runner at 5 m/s, or a 1,200-kg car rolling at 0.25 m/s?
  3. A 4-kg cart moving at 6 m/s hits a 2-kg cart at rest. They stick together. What is their speed afterward?
steps: 1. p = 0.5 × 12 = 6 kg·m/s
2. Runner: 70 × 5 = 350. Car: 1,200 × 0.25 = 300. The runner has more.
3. Before: 4 × 6 = 24 kg·m/s. After: 24 ÷ (4 + 2) = 4 m/s

notes.say: Last independent round. Number 2 is a surprise for most people: the car is far heavier, but it is barely moving. Do the multiplication before you decide. For number 3, use the three-move routine from the car crash.
ask: Read me your answers. (expected answer: 6 kg·m/s; the runner, 350 vs. 300; 4 m/s)
notes.answer: 1. 6 kg·m/s. 2. The runner (350 kg·m/s vs. 300 kg·m/s). 3. 4 m/s.
notes.watch: On number 3, the most common wrong answer is 6 m/s (forgetting the added mass) or 12 m/s (dividing 24 by 2 kg). The combined mass is 6 kg.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Speed-Time Graph
slides.board:
The graph shows a runner's speed during a short race.

Which statement best describes the runner's motion from 4 s to 8 s?

A. The runner is stopped, because the line is flat.
B. The runner moves at a constant speed of 8 m/s.
C. The runner speeds up by 8 m/s every second.
D. The runner is slowing down to finish the race.
steps: A is out. Flat means stopped only on a distance-time graph. This y-axis is speed, and the speed is 8 m/s, not 0.
C is out. Speeding up would need a line sloping up. From 4 to 8 s the speed stays at 8; the acceleration is 0. (8 m/s is a speed, not a change per second.)
D is out. Slowing down shows as a line sloping down, which happens only after 8 s.
B is correct. The line is flat at 8 m/s, so the speed is constant at 8 m/s.

notes.say: This is the most common physics graph question on the GED. The trap choice is A, and it is there on purpose for anyone who skips the axis label. Read the label, then eliminate each wrong choice out loud with a reason.
ask: What was the runner's acceleration from 0 to 4 s? (expected answer: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m/s<sup>2</sup>)
notes.answer: B. On a speed-time graph a flat line means constant speed; here it is 8 m/s. A misreads the graph as distance-time; C confuses a speed with an acceleration; D describes 8–10 s.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Newton's Laws
slides.board:
A 70-kg skater and a 35-kg skater stand face to face on smooth ice. They push off each other and glide apart.

Which statement is correct?

A. The 70-kg skater pushes with the greater force, because he has more mass.
B. The forces on the two skaters are equal in size, so the 35-kg skater accelerates more.
C. The two forces are equal and opposite, so they cancel and neither skater moves.
D. Only the skater who pushes harder moves; the other one stays in place.
steps: A is out. By the third law, the force pair is always equal in size, no matter the masses.
C is out. The two forces act on different skaters, so they do not cancel. Each skater has an unbalanced force and accelerates.
D is out. Both feel a force, so both move, in opposite directions.
B is correct. Equal forces, but a = F ÷ m: half the mass means twice the acceleration for the 35-kg skater.

notes.say: This question mixes the third and second laws, which the GED likes to do. The third law tells you the forces are equal. The second law tells you the lighter skater gets the bigger acceleration. Choice C is the classic misconception; knock it out by saying 'different objects.'
ask: If the 35-kg skater glides off at 2 m/s, how fast does the 70-kg skater move? (stretch, expected answer: 1 m/s; momentum 35 × 2 = 70 must match 70 × 1)
notes.answer: B. Third law: equal and opposite forces. Second law: the lighter skater has the larger acceleration. A and D deny the equal pair; C wrongly cancels forces that act on different objects.

slides.title: Test Strategy: The Formula Routine
slides.board:
1. Find the formula in the question or stimulus (the GED usually gives it).
  2. List each number with its unit.
  3. Convert units to match (60 min = 1 h; 1,000 g = 1 kg).
  4. Calculate with the on-screen calculator.
  5. Check: right unit? reasonable size?

Wrong choices are built from skipped steps: multiplying instead of dividing, using one force instead of the net force, skipping a conversion.

notes.say: The GED Science test gives you a calculator and usually prints the formula in the question, so the test is not about memorizing. It is about running a clean routine. When you see your answer choices, notice that the wrong ones are the numbers you get from a skipped step. If your answer matches a choice, take two seconds to check the unit and the size before you click.
ask: A choice says 0.4 m/s<sup>2</sup> and you know the force is 20 N and the mass is 50 kg. Is that right? (expected answer: yes, 20 ÷ 50 = 0.4; but 2.5 would be the trap from dividing 50 by 20)

slides.board:
1. Speed = d ÷ t; velocity adds direction; acceleration = change in speed ÷ time.
  2. Read the y-axis: flat on distance-time = stopped; flat on speed-time = constant speed.

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
Physics is the science of how things move and why. On the GED Science test, physical science is about 40 percent of the questions, and motion and forces are a favorite topic. The test usually gives you the formula and an on-screen calculator. What it checks is whether you can pick the right numbers, keep the units straight, and read a motion graph. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • Calculate speed, velocity, and acceleration.
  • Read distance-time and speed-time graphs.
  • Find the net force and use Newton's three laws and F = ma.
  • Calculate work and power, and explain how simple machines help.
  • Calculate momentum and predict the result of a simple collision.

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Keep a calculator and scratch paper handy, and start a formula card as you go.

screens.title: Speed
screens.html:
Speed tells how fast something moves. It is the distance traveled divided by the time it took:

speed = distance ÷ time    (s = d ÷ t)

The unit always reads "distance per time": meters per second (m/s), kilometers per hour (km/h), miles per hour (mi/h). The word per means "divided by," so the distance goes on top.

You can turn the formula around: distance = speed × time and time = distance ÷ speed.

Most speeds you calculate are average speeds. A car that goes 120 miles in 2 hours averages 60 mi/h, even if it sped up and slowed down along the way.

example.prompt: A delivery driver travels 150 miles in 3 hours. What is her average speed? At that speed, how far would she go in 5 hours?
steps: Speed: s = d ÷ t = 150 mi ÷ 3 h = 50 mi/h.
Distance: d = s × t = 50 mi/h × 5 h = 250 mi.

check.prompt: A sprinter runs 100 meters in 12.5 seconds. What is her average speed, in meters per second?

mistakes.why: You divided time by distance (12.5 ÷ 100). Speed is distance divided by time: 100 m ÷ 12.5 s.
You multiplied distance and time. Speed is distance divided by time: 100 ÷ 12.5 = 8.

check.hint: Speed = distance ÷ time. Put the meters on top.
check.explain:
s = d ÷ t = 100 m ÷ 12.5 s = 8 m/s.

The unit m/s means meters divided by seconds, which tells you the order. Dividing 12.5 by 100 gives 0.125, which would be seconds per meter, not a speed.

screens.title: Units and average speed
screens.html:
Before you calculate, make the units match the question. If the question asks for km/h but the time is in minutes, convert the minutes to hours first: hours = minutes ÷ 60.

Minutes1520304590
Hours0.251/30.50.751.5

Average speed for a whole trip = total distance ÷ total time. Stops count as part of the total time, even though no distance is covered during them.

example.prompt: A cyclist rides 6 km in 15 minutes, rests for 5 minutes, then rides 4 km in 10 minutes. What is her average speed for the whole trip, in km/h?
steps: Total distance: 6 + 4 = 10 km.
Total time, including the rest: 15 + 5 + 10 = 30 min = 0.5 h.
Average speed: 10 km ÷ 0.5 h = 20 km/h.

check.prompt: A commuter train travels 36 km in 45 minutes. What is its average speed in kilometers per hour?

mistakes.why: 0.8 is the speed in kilometers per minute (36 ÷ 45). The question asks for km/h, so convert 45 minutes to 0.75 hours first.
You multiplied 36 by 0.75. Speed is distance divided by time: 36 km ÷ 0.75 h.

check.hint: Change 45 minutes into hours first (divide by 60).
check.explain:
Convert: 45 min ÷ 60 = 0.75 h.

s = 36 km ÷ 0.75 h = 48 km/h.

Check: in 15 minutes the train goes 12 km, so in 60 minutes it goes 4 × 12 = 48 km. The tempting answer 0.8 is correct arithmetic in the wrong unit (km per minute).

screens.title: Speed versus velocity
screens.html:
Velocity is speed with a direction: 15 m/s east, 60 mi/h north. Speed answers "how fast?" Velocity answers "how fast, and which way?"

  • Two runners at 5 m/s, one going east and one going west, have the same speed but different velocities.
  • A car going around a curve at a steady 30 mi/h has a constant speed but a changing velocity, because its direction keeps changing.

A change in velocity, whether in speed or direction, is called acceleration. You will calculate it on the next screen.

check.prompt: Which description gives a velocity rather than only a speed?
options: A jet flying at 800 km/h toward the west
A jet flying at a steady 800 km/h
A jet that flew 800 km in one hour
A jet with a top speed of 900 km/h
why: "Steady" tells you the speed is not changing, but it gives no direction. A velocity needs a direction, such as "toward the west."
This gives a distance and a time, which let you find the speed (800 km/h), but no direction. Velocity needs a direction.
A top speed is still just a speed. Velocity needs a direction, such as north or west.
check.hint: Velocity = speed + direction. Which choice names a direction?
check.explain: Only "800 km/h toward the west" includes a direction, so it is the only velocity. The other choices describe how fast the jet goes but not which way, so they give speed only.

screens.title: Acceleration
screens.html:
Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes:

acceleration = (final speed − starting speed) ÷ time

The unit is m/s2, read "meters per second squared" or "meters per second, every second." An acceleration of 3 m/s2 means the speed grows by 3 m/s each second.

  • Speeding up: positive acceleration.
  • Slowing down: negative acceleration (sometimes called deceleration).
  • Changing direction: also acceleration, even at a steady speed.
  • Constant velocity: zero acceleration.

Always subtract final minus starting, and divide by the length of time the change took.

example.prompt: A car at a red light starts from rest. When the light turns green, it reaches 18 m/s in 6 s. What is its acceleration?
steps: "Starts from rest" means the starting speed is 0 m/s.
a = (18 − 0) ÷ 6 = 18 ÷ 6 = 3 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

check.prompt: A skateboarder rolling at 3 m/s speeds up to 11 m/s in 4 seconds. What is her acceleration, in m/s2?

mistakes.why: You divided the final speed by the time (11 ÷ 4) and ignored the starting speed. Acceleration uses the change in speed: 11 − 3 = 8.
You added the speeds (11 + 3 = 14) before dividing. Acceleration uses the change: final minus starting, 11 − 3 = 8, then 8 ÷ 4.
8 m/s is the change in speed. You still need to divide by the 4 seconds it took: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

check.hint: Find how much the speed changed, then divide by the time.
check.explain:
Change in speed: 11 m/s − 3 m/s = 8 m/s.

a = 8 m/s ÷ 4 s = 2 m/s2.

Check: 3 → 5 → 7 → 9 → 11 m/s over 4 seconds, gaining 2 m/s each second.

screens.title: Distance-time graphs
screens.html:
A distance-time graph puts time on the x-axis and distance on the y-axis. Read its shape like this:

  • Flat line: the distance is not changing, so the object is stopped.
  • Straight line sloping up: moving at a constant speed. A steeper line means a faster speed.
  • Line sloping down: moving back toward the starting point.

The slope of the line is the speed: change in distance ÷ change in time. The graph below shows a walk with a short stop.

example.prompt: Use the graph. What was the walker's speed from 15 to 25 minutes?
steps: Read the distances: 600 m at 15 min and 1,600 m at 25 min.
Change in distance: 1,600 − 600 = 1,000 m. Change in time: 25 − 15 = 10 min.
Speed = 1,000 m ÷ 10 min = 100 m/min.
example.answer: 100 m/min (faster than the 60 m/min from 0 to 10 minutes; the line is steeper)

check.prompt: Use the walker's graph. During which interval was the walker not moving?
why: From 0 to 10 minutes the distance rises from 0 to 600 m, so the walker is moving. Look for the part where the line is flat.
From 15 to 25 minutes the line climbs steeply, from 600 m to 1,600 m. That is the fastest part of the walk, not a stop.
From 5 to 10 minutes the distance rises from 300 m to 600 m, so the walker is moving. A stop shows as a flat line.
check.hint: On a distance-time graph, what does the line look like when the distance does not change?
check.explain: The line is flat at 600 m from 10 to 15 minutes, so the distance did not change and the walker was stopped. (The graph is also flat from 25 to 30 minutes, after the walker arrived, but that interval is not a choice.) Every other choice is a time when the line rises, so the walker was moving.

screens.title: Speed-time graphs
screens.html:
A speed-time graph puts speed on the y-axis. The same shapes mean different things here:

  • Flat line: the speed is not changing, so the object moves at a constant speed. (Only a flat line at 0 means stopped.)
  • Sloping up: speeding up.
  • Sloping down: slowing down.

The slope of a speed-time graph is the acceleration. Always read the y-axis label before you decide what a flat line means.

The graph shows an elevator moving between floors.

check.prompt:
Use the elevator graph. Complete the statements.

From 0 to 2 s, the elevator is {{0}}. From 2 to 4 s, the elevator is {{1}}. From 4 to 6 s, its acceleration is {{2}}.

why: The speed rises from 0 to 3 m/s, so it is moving, not stopped. A stopped elevator has a speed of 0.
The line slopes up from 0 to 3 m/s, so the speed is changing. Constant speed is a flat line.
The speed goes up, from 0 to 3 m/s. Slowing down shows as a line sloping down.

options: moving at a constant speed of 3 m/s
speeding up by 3 m/s every second
why: A flat line means stopped only on a distance-time graph. This y-axis is speed, and the speed is 3 m/s, not 0.
3 m/s is the speed, not a change per second. The flat line means the speed is not changing, so the acceleration is 0.
The speed stays at 3 m/s from 2 to 4 s. Slowing down happens only after 4 s, where the line slopes down.
The size is right, but the elevator is slowing down (3 to 0 m/s), so the change in speed is negative: (0 − 3) ÷ 2.
−3 m/s is the change in speed. Divide it by the 2 seconds the slowdown took: −3 ÷ 2 = −1.5 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
The speed changes from 3 m/s to 0, so the acceleration is not zero. Zero acceleration is a flat line.

check.hint: Read the y-axis: this graph shows speed. Then use a = (final − starting) ÷ time for the last part.
check.explain:
0–2 s: the line slopes up, so the elevator is speeding up (from 0 to 3 m/s).

2–4 s: the line is flat at 3 m/s, so it moves at a constant speed of 3 m/s. It is not stopped; this is a speed-time graph.

4–6 s: a = (0 − 3) ÷ (6 − 4) = −3 ÷ 2 = −1.5 m/s2 (slowing down).

screens.title: Forces and net force
screens.html:
A force is a push or a pull. Forces are measured in newtons (N). Gravity, friction, air resistance, and a hand pushing a cart are all forces.

When several forces act on one object, find the net force, their combined effect:

  • Forces in the same direction add.
  • Forces in opposite directions subtract, and the net force points toward the larger force.

If the net force is zero, the forces are balanced and the object's motion does not change. If the net force is not zero, the forces are unbalanced and the object accelerates in the direction of the net force.

Tip: draw an arrow for each force before you combine them.

example.prompt: In a tug-of-war, Team 1 pulls left with 600 N. Team 2 pulls right with 450 N. What is the net force on the rope?
steps: The forces point in opposite directions, so subtract: 600 − 450 = 150 N.
The net force points toward the larger force: 150 N to the left. The rope (and Team 2) will accelerate to the left.

check.prompt: Two movers push a couch to the right, one with 140 N and one with 110 N. Friction acts on the couch to the left with 170 N. What is the size of the net force on the couch, in newtons?

mistakes.why: You added all three forces. Friction points the opposite way, so subtract it: 140 + 110 − 170.
250 N is the movers' total push. Friction (170 N) acts in the opposite direction and must be subtracted.
You subtracted only one mover's force (140 − 110) and left out friction. Add the two pushes that point the same way, then subtract friction.

check.hint: Add the forces that point the same way. Then subtract the force that points the other way.
check.explain:
Same direction (right): 140 N + 110 N = 250 N.

Opposite direction (left): 250 N − 170 N = 80 N, pointing to the right.

Because the net force is not zero, the forces are unbalanced and the couch accelerates to the right.

screens.title: Newton's first law: inertia
screens.html:
Newton's first law: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line, unless an unbalanced force acts on it.

This tendency to resist a change in motion is called inertia. More mass means more inertia: a loaded truck is harder to start and harder to stop than a bicycle.

  • When a bus brakes suddenly, riders lurch forward. Their bodies keep moving forward until the seat or a seat belt pushes on them.
  • A hockey puck slides a long way on smooth ice because almost no friction acts on it.
  • A car moving at a steady speed on a straight road has balanced forces: the net force is zero, even though the car is moving.

check.prompt: A truck carries a box in its open bed. When the truck suddenly speeds up, the box slides toward the back of the bed. Which statement best explains this?
options: The box tends to stay at its original speed while the truck speeds up beneath it.
A backward force from the engine pushes the box toward the rear of the truck.
The box has less mass than the truck, so it must accelerate backward.
The truck bed pushes back on the box with an equal and opposite force.
why: The engine pushes the truck forward, not the box backward. The box only seems to move back because the truck moves forward under it.
Less mass does not make an object move backward. With nothing pushing it forward hard enough, the box simply lags behind as the truck speeds up.
This mixes up the third law. Action-reaction pairs act on two different objects; they do not explain why the box falls behind. Inertia does.
check.hint: Think about inertia: what does an object tend to do when nothing pushes it?
check.explain: This is Newton's first law. The box tends to keep moving at the speed it had. When the truck speeds up, friction is not strong enough to speed the box up as quickly, so the truck moves forward beneath it and the box ends up nearer the back. No backward force is needed; the box is just resisting a change in its motion.

screens.title: Newton's second law: F = ma
screens.html:
Newton's second law connects force, mass, and acceleration:

F = m × a    a = F ÷ m    m = F ÷ a

  • F is the net force in newtons (N).
  • m is the mass in kilograms (kg).
  • a is the acceleration in m/s2.

More force gives more acceleration. More mass gives less acceleration for the same force. That is why a full shopping cart is harder to get moving than an empty one.

One newton is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s2: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s2.

example.prompt: A net force of 600 N acts on a 150-kg motorcycle. What is its acceleration?
steps: Solve for a: a = F ÷ m.
a = 600 N ÷ 150 kg = 4 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

check.prompt: A tow truck pulls a 1,200-kg car. The net force on the car is 3,000 N. What is the car's acceleration, in m/s2?

mistakes.why: You divided mass by force (1,200 ÷ 3,000). Acceleration is force divided by mass: a = F ÷ m.
You multiplied force and mass. F = ma means a = F ÷ m, so divide: 3,000 ÷ 1,200.

check.hint: Rearrange F = ma to get a by itself.
check.explain:
a = F ÷ m = 3,000 N ÷ 1,200 kg = 2.5 m/s2.

Check: 1,200 kg × 2.5 m/s2 = 3,000 N. Dividing the other way (1,200 ÷ 3,000 = 0.4) is the most common slip.

screens.title: Mass and weight
screens.html:
Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. It is the same everywhere: on Earth, on the Moon, or in space.

Weight is a force: the pull of gravity on an object. Because it is a force, weight is measured in newtons. It is a special case of F = ma:

weight = mass × g    (on Earth, g ≈ 9.8 m/s2)

On the Moon, gravity is weaker (g ≈ 1.6 m/s2), so your weight is about one-sixth as much, but your mass does not change.

example.prompt: A suitcase has a mass of 20 kg. What does it weigh on Earth?
steps: weight = m × g = 20 kg × 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
weight = 196 N.

check.prompt: An astronaut has a mass of 75 kg. Use g = 9.8 m/s2. What is her weight on Earth, in newtons?

mistakes.why: 75 is her mass in kilograms. Weight is a force: multiply the mass by g, 75 × 9.8.
You divided 75 by 9.8. Weight = mass × g, so multiply.

check.explain:
weight = m × g = 75 kg × 9.8 m/s2 = 735 N.

Her mass is 75 kg everywhere. Her weight depends on gravity: on the Moon it would be only about 75 × 1.6 = 120 N.

screens.title: Newton's third law: action and reaction
screens.html:
Newton's third law: When object A pushes on object B, object B pushes back on object A with a force that is equal in size and opposite in direction.

  • A swimmer pushes the water backward; the water pushes the swimmer forward.
  • A rocket pushes hot gas downward; the gas pushes the rocket upward.
  • You push the floor backward with your foot; the floor pushes you forward.

Key point: the two forces act on two different objects, so they do not cancel each other. To find whether one object accelerates, combine only the forces acting on that object.

Equal forces do not mean equal accelerations. By the second law, the object with less mass gets the bigger acceleration.

check.prompt: A bug hits the windshield of a moving car. How does the force of the windshield on the bug compare with the force of the bug on the windshield?
options: The two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.
The windshield pushes far harder, because the car has far more mass.
The bug pushes harder, because the bug is the object that gets crushed.
Only the windshield exerts a force; the bug is too small to push back.
why: Mass affects acceleration, not the size of the force pair. By the third law, the forces are always equal; the bug's tiny mass is why its acceleration is so huge.
Being crushed shows the bug has a huge acceleration and a fragile body, not a bigger force. The third law says the two forces are equal.
Every force comes in a pair. If the windshield pushes the bug, the bug pushes the windshield back just as hard (third law).
check.hint: Third law: every push comes with an equal push back.
check.explain: By Newton's third law, the forces are equal in size and opposite in direction. The results are very different because of the second law: the same force on the bug's tiny mass gives it an enormous acceleration (a = F ÷ m), while the car's huge mass barely changes its motion. The tempting answer "the windshield pushes harder" confuses a bigger effect with a bigger force.

screens.title: Work
screens.html:
In physics, work is done when a force moves an object in the direction of the force:

work = force × distance    (W = F × d)

Work is measured in joules (J). 1 J = 1 N × 1 m.

No movement means no work. Holding a heavy bag still, or pushing on a wall that does not move, does zero work on the object, even if you get tired. Carrying a bag across a flat room at a steady height also does no work on the bag by your upward holding force, because the bag does not move up.

When you lift something, the force you need equals its weight, and the distance is the height.

example.prompt: A worker lifts a 250-N bag of cement 1.2 m onto a truck. How much work does she do?
steps: Force = weight = 250 N; distance = height = 1.2 m.

check.prompt: In which two situations is work done on the object named? Select two answers.
options: A parent lifts a toddler from the floor up to her hip.
A student pushes a stalled car 5 meters along a level street.
A guard stands holding a heavy flag perfectly still for an hour.
A climber pushes hard against a boulder that does not budge.
A waiter holds a tray steady while standing in one spot.
why: The flag does not move, so the distance is zero and the work is zero, no matter how tiring it feels.
The boulder does not move, so d = 0 and W = F × 0 = 0. Effort alone is not work in physics.
The tray stays in one place. No distance in the direction of the force means no work.
check.hint: Work needs a force and movement in the direction of the force.
check.explain: Work = force × distance. Lifting the toddler moves her upward, in the direction of the lifting force, and pushing the car moves it forward, in the direction of the push, so work is done in both. The flag, the boulder, and the tray do not move, so d = 0 and no work is done on them, even though the people holding or pushing get tired.

screens.title: Power
screens.html:
Power is how fast work is done:

power = work ÷ time    (P = W ÷ t)

Power is measured in watts (W). 1 W = 1 joule per second.

Two people who lift the same box to the same shelf do the same work. The one who does it faster uses more power. Half the time means twice the power.

Careful: in the formula, W stands for work (joules). As a unit, W stands for watts. Read the units to tell them apart.

Finding power usually takes two steps: find the work (F × d), then divide by the time.

example.prompt: A motor lifts a 500-N load 6 m in 10 s. What is its power?
steps: Work: W = 500 N × 6 m = 3,000 J.
Power: P = 3,000 J ÷ 10 s = 300 W.

check.prompt: A student carries a 450-N backpack up a staircase 4 m high in 12 s. What power does she use to raise the backpack, in watts?

mistakes.why: 1,800 J is the work (450 × 4). Power is work divided by time: 1,800 ÷ 12.
You multiplied the work by the time. Power is work divided by time: 1,800 J ÷ 12 s.
You divided the force by the time (450 ÷ 12) and left out the height. First find the work: 450 N × 4 m = 1,800 J; then divide by 12 s.

check.hint: Find the work first (force × height). Then divide by the time.
check.explain:
Work: W = F × d = 450 N × 4 m = 1,800 J.

Power: P = W ÷ t = 1,800 J ÷ 12 s = 150 W.

screens.title: Simple machines and mechanical advantage
screens.html:
A simple machine makes a job easier by changing the size or direction of a force. The six simple machines are the lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane (ramp), wedge, and screw.

A machine does not reduce the work. It lets you use less force over a longer distance. In an ideal machine (no friction), work in = work out.

mechanical advantage (MA) = output force ÷ input force

Ramp: ideal MA = length ÷ height

To find the push needed on a ramp: find the work to lift the load straight up (weight × height), then divide by the ramp length.

example.prompt: A 400-N box is pushed up a 3-m ramp onto a porch 0.6 m high. Ignoring friction, what push is needed, and what is the MA?

figure.alt: A ramp drawn as a right triangle. The sloped side is labeled 3 m. The vertical side is labeled 0.6 m. A box labeled 400 N sits at the bottom of the ramp.

steps: Work to lift straight up: 400 N × 0.6 m = 240 J.
Same work along the ramp: F × 3 m = 240 J, so F = 240 ÷ 3 = 80 N.
MA = 400 N ÷ 80 N = 5. Check: 3 m ÷ 0.6 m = 5.

check.prompt: A 1,000-N motorcycle is pushed up a 4-m ramp into a truck bed 0.8 m high. Ignoring friction, how much force must be applied along the ramp, in newtons?

mistakes.why: 800 J is the work to lift the motorcycle straight up (1,000 × 0.8). Spread that work over the 4-m ramp: 800 ÷ 4.
You divided the weight by the ramp length (1,000 ÷ 4) and left out the height. Work = 1,000 × 0.8 = 800 J; then 800 ÷ 4 = 200 N.
You multiplied the weight by the MA instead of dividing. A ramp reduces the force: 1,000 N ÷ 5 = 200 N.

check.hint: Find the work to lift it straight up, then divide by the ramp length.
check.explain:
Work to lift straight up: 1,000 N × 0.8 m = 800 J.

Along the ramp: F × 4 m = 800 J, so F = 800 ÷ 4 = 200 N.

Check with MA: 4 m ÷ 0.8 m = 5, and 1,000 N ÷ 5 = 200 N.

screens.title: Levers and pulleys
screens.html:
A lever is a bar that turns on a pivot point called the fulcrum. The effort arm is the distance from the fulcrum to where you push; the load arm is the distance from the fulcrum to the load.

Lever: ideal MA = effort arm ÷ load arm

Moving the fulcrum closer to the load makes the load arm shorter and the MA bigger, so the job takes less force.

Pulley setupIdeal MAWhat it does
Single fixed pulley1changes direction only (pull down to lift up)
Single movable pulley2halves the force; you pull twice as much rope

example.prompt: A crowbar pivots 0.1 m from a nail and is pushed 0.5 m from the pivot. The nail resists with 900 N. What is the ideal effort force?
steps: MA = effort arm ÷ load arm = 0.5 ÷ 0.1 = 5.
Effort = load ÷ MA = 900 N ÷ 5 = 180 N.

check.prompt: A gardener uses a 2-m pole as a lever to lift a stump. Which fulcrum position gives her the greatest mechanical advantage?
options: 0.25 m from the stump, so she pushes 1.75 m from the fulcrum
1.0 m from the stump, so she pushes 1.0 m from the fulcrum
0.5 m from the stump, so she pushes 1.5 m from the fulcrum
1.5 m from the stump, so she pushes 0.5 m from the fulcrum
why: Equal arms give MA = 1.0 ÷ 1.0 = 1, so the lever does not reduce her force at all.
MA = 1.5 ÷ 0.5 = 3. That helps, but a fulcrum even closer to the stump gives a larger MA.
Here the load arm is longer than the effort arm: MA = 0.5 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 0.33. She would need more force than the stump's weight.
check.hint: MA = effort arm ÷ load arm. The stump is the load.
check.explain:
Compute MA = effort arm ÷ load arm for each position:

  • 0.25 m from the stump: 1.75 ÷ 0.25 = 7
  • 0.5 m: 1.5 ÷ 0.5 = 3
  • 1.0 m: 1.0 ÷ 1.0 = 1
  • 1.5 m: 0.5 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 0.33

The fulcrum closest to the stump gives the greatest MA. The trade-off: her end of the pole must move 7 times as far as the stump rises.

screens.title: Momentum
screens.html:
Momentum is "mass in motion." It measures how hard it is to stop a moving object:

momentum = mass × velocity    (p = m × v)

The unit is kg·m/s. Momentum has a direction, the same direction as the velocity.

  • An object that is not moving has zero momentum, however heavy it is.
  • A light, fast object and a heavy, slow object can have the same momentum: a 0.2-kg ball at 30 m/s and a 3-kg ball at 2 m/s both have 6 kg·m/s.

To compare momentum, always multiply mass by velocity. Do not judge by speed or mass alone.

options: A 0.06-kg tennis ball moving at 50 m/s
A 2,000-kg truck parked at the curb
A 5-kg bowling ball moving at 6 m/s
why: The ball is the fastest object, but its mass is tiny: 0.06 × 50 = 3 kg·m/s. Momentum depends on mass and velocity together.
The truck is the heaviest, but it is parked. With v = 0, its momentum is 2,000 × 0 = 0.
5 × 6 = 30 kg·m/s, which is less than the cyclist's 60 × 8 = 480 kg·m/s.
check.hint: Multiply mass × velocity for each object.
check.explain:
p = m × v:

  • Cyclist: 60 × 8 = 480 kg·m/s
  • Bowling ball: 5 × 6 = 30
  • Tennis ball: 0.06 × 50 = 3
  • Parked truck: 2,000 × 0 = 0

The heaviest object has no momentum because it is not moving, and the fastest object has very little because its mass is so small.

screens.title: Conservation of momentum
screens.html:
When objects collide and no outside force (like friction) interferes, momentum is conserved:

total momentum before = total momentum after

Momentum is not lost in a collision; it is shared or passed along. For two objects that stick together, use three moves:

  1. Add up the momentum before: m1v1 + m2v2.
  2. Add the masses: the objects now move as one.
  3. Divide: speed after = total momentum ÷ total mass.

Because the same momentum is shared by more mass, the joined objects move slower than the first object did.

example.prompt: A 3-kg cart moving at 4 m/s runs into a 1-kg cart at rest. They stick together. How fast do they move?
steps: Before: (3 × 4) + (1 × 0) = 12 kg·m/s.
Mass after: 3 + 1 = 4 kg.
Speed after: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 m/s.

check.prompt: An 80-kg football player running at 6 m/s tackles a 70-kg player who is standing still. They move together after the tackle. Ignoring friction, what is their speed just after the tackle, in m/s?

mistakes.why: 6 m/s ignores the second player's mass. The same momentum (480 kg·m/s) is now shared by 150 kg, so the speed must drop: 480 ÷ 150.
480 kg·m/s is the total momentum, not a speed. Divide it by the combined mass, 80 + 70 = 150 kg.
You divided the momentum by only the second player's mass (480 ÷ 70). After the tackle both players move together, so divide by 150 kg.

check.hint: Momentum before = 80 × 6. After the tackle, the moving mass is 80 + 70.
check.explain:
Before: (80 × 6) + (70 × 0) = 480 kg·m/s.

Mass after: 80 + 70 = 150 kg.

v = 480 ÷ 150 = 3.2 m/s.

The answer must be less than 6 m/s, because the same momentum is spread over more mass.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Speed = distance ÷ time. Velocity = speed + direction. Convert units first (min ÷ 60 = h).
  • Acceleration = (final − starting speed) ÷ time, in m/s2. Negative = slowing down.
  • Graphs: read the y-axis. Distance-time: flat = stopped, slope = speed. Speed-time: flat = constant speed, slope = acceleration.
  • Net force: same direction add, opposite subtract. Zero net force = balanced = no change in motion.
  • Newton's laws: 1st inertia; 2nd F = ma (net force); 3rd equal and opposite forces on two different objects.
  • Weight = m × g (g ≈ 9.8 m/s2), in newtons.
  • Work W = F × d (J), only if the object moves. Power P = W ÷ t (W).
  • Machines trade less force for more distance; work stays the same. MA = output ÷ input force; ramp = length ÷ height; lever = effort arm ÷ load arm.
  • Momentum p = m × v; total before = total after.

Routine for every physics calculation: formula → numbers with units → convert → calculate → check the unit and size.

Next, go to Practice and start with Set A.
