items.prompt: Two cars pass each other on a straight highway. One heads north at 65 mi/h. The other heads south at 65 mi/h. Which statement is true?
options: They have the same speed but different velocities.
They have the same velocity, because their speeds are equal.
They have different speeds, because they travel in opposite directions.
Neither car has a velocity, because neither car is speeding up.
why: Equal speeds are not enough for equal velocities. Velocity includes direction, and these cars head in opposite directions.
Direction does not change speed. Both cars cover 65 miles each hour, so their speeds are the same; only their directions differ.
You mixed up velocity and acceleration. Every moving object has a velocity (speed plus direction); speeding up is acceleration.
items.hint: Velocity = speed + direction.
items.explain: Both cars move at 65 mi/h, so their speeds are the same. Velocity is speed with a direction, and one car goes north while the other goes south, so their velocities are different. Saying the velocities are equal ignores the direction, which is the whole difference between speed and velocity.

items.prompt: During which time interval was the cyclist stopped at the traffic light?
why: From 0 to 4 minutes the distance rises from 0 to 2 km, so she is moving. A stop shows as a flat line.
From 8 to 12 minutes the line climbs from 2 km to 5 km; that is the fastest part of the trip, not the stop.
From 10 to 12 minutes the distance rises from 3.5 km to 5 km, so she is moving. Look for the flat part of the line.
items.hint: On a distance-time graph, what does the line look like when the distance is not changing?
items.explain:
On a distance-time graph, a flat line means the distance is not changing, so the object is stopped. From 4 to 8 minutes, the distance stays at 2 km. The cyclist is stopped.

During 0–4 minutes and 8–12 minutes, the line slopes upward, so her distance from home is increasing. She is moving during those times.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the car's motion from 6 seconds to 10 seconds?
options: The car moves at a constant speed of 18 m/s.
The car is stopped, because the line on the graph is flat.
The car is speeding up by 18 m/s every second.
The car is slowing down until it comes to rest.
why: A flat line means stopped only on a distance-time graph. This y-axis shows speed, and the speed is 18 m/s, not 0.
18 m/s is the speed, not a change per second. The line is flat, so the speed is not changing and the acceleration is 0.
Slowing down would show as a line sloping down toward 0. From 6 to 10 s the line stays level at 18 m/s.
items.hint: Read the y-axis label. This graph shows speed, not distance.
items.explain:
This is a speed-time graph. From 6 s to 10 s, the line is flat at 18 m/s, so the speed is not changing. The car moves at a constant speed of 18 m/s.

"Stopped" is the most common wrong answer. A flat line means stopped only on a distance-time graph. A stopped car would have a speed of 0 m/s, with the line on the x-axis.

items.prompt: During which part of the trip was the cyclist moving fastest?
options: She moved at the same speed for the whole trip.
why: From 0 to 4 minutes she covered 2 km in 4 min (0.5 km/min). From 8 to 12 minutes she covered 3 km in 4 min, which is faster. The steeper line is faster.
From 4 to 8 minutes the line is flat: she was stopped at the light, so her speed was 0.
Her speed changed: 0.5 km/min, then 0 during the stop, then 0.75 km/min. The line has different steepness in different parts.
items.hint: On a distance-time graph, the steeper the line, the faster the motion. Or calculate the speed for each part.
items.explain:
Calculate the speed for each moving part using speed = distance ÷ time:

  • 0 to 4 min: (2 km − 0 km) ÷ 4 min = 0.5 km/min
  • 8 to 12 min: (5 km − 2 km) ÷ 4 min = 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75 km/min

0.75 km/min is greater, so she was fastest from 8 to 12 minutes. The line is steepest there. From 4 to 8 minutes she was stopped, and her speed was clearly not the same for the whole trip.

items.prompt: What was the cyclist's average speed, in kilometers per hour, for the entire 12-minute trip, including the stop?

mistakes.why: 5 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.42 is the speed in km per minute. The question asks for km/h: convert 12 minutes to 0.2 hour first.
You left out the 4-minute stop (5 km ÷ 8 min). The question asks about the entire trip, so use the total time, 12 minutes.
You multiplied 5 km by 12. Average speed is total distance divided by total time: 5 km ÷ 0.2 h.

items.hint: Use total distance ÷ total time. Convert 12 minutes to hours first (60 minutes = 1 hour).
items.explain:
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.

Total distance = 5 km. Total time = 12 min = 12 ÷ 60 = 0.2 h.

Average speed = 5 km ÷ 0.2 h = 25 km/h.

Common errors: 5 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.42 is in km per minute, not km/h. Leaving out the 4-minute stop (5 km ÷ 8 min = 0.625 km/min = 37.5 km/h) is also wrong, because the question asks about the entire trip.

items.prompt: Acceleration is calculated using the formula a = (final speed − starting speed) ÷ time. What was the car's acceleration from 0 seconds to 6 seconds, in m/s2?

mistakes.why: You divided 18 by 10, the length of the whole test. The car sped up only from 0 to 6 s, so divide the change in speed by 6 s.
18 m/s is the change in speed. Divide it by the 6 seconds it took: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
6 m/s is how much the speed rises in each 2-second step on the graph. Per second, that is 6 ÷ 2 = 3 m/s2.

items.hint: Read the speed at 0 s and at 6 s from the graph.
items.explain:
At 0 s the speed is 0 m/s. At 6 s the speed is 18 m/s.

a = (18 m/s − 0 m/s) ÷ 6 s = 18 ÷ 6 = 3 m/s2

Check with any 2-second step on the graph: the speed rises by 6 m/s every 2 s, which is 3 m/s each second. Dividing 18 by 10 (the whole test) is wrong, because the car was not speeding up after 6 s.

items.prompt: Drag each example into the box for the law of motion it best illustrates.
choices: A passenger lurches forward when a bus stops suddenly.
A hockey puck slides across smooth ice in a straight line until it hits the boards.
The same push gives an empty shopping cart a greater acceleration than a full one.
A loaded truck needs a larger net force than a small car to reach the same acceleration.
A rocket pushes exhaust gases downward, and the gases push the rocket upward.
A swimmer pushes backward on the pool wall and moves forward.
items.why: The most common slip is putting the passenger or the puck under the second law because they involve motion. Ask: is the object just continuing what it was doing (first law), is force compared with mass and acceleration (second law), or are two objects pushing on each other (third law)?
items.hint: First law: objects keep doing what they were doing. Second law: force, mass, and acceleration. Third law: a pair of pushes between two objects.
items.explain:
First law (inertia): The passenger keeps moving forward when the bus stops, and the puck keeps sliding in a straight line because nearly nothing acts to stop it until the boards do. Both show objects continuing their motion.

Second law (F = ma): The empty cart has less mass, so the same force gives more acceleration (a = F ÷ m). The truck has more mass, so it needs more force for the same acceleration (F = ma).

Third law: The rocket and gases push on each other in opposite directions; the swimmer and wall push on each other in opposite directions. Each example is a pair of equal and opposite forces on two different objects.

items.prompt:
Two people push on a 10-kg box resting on a smooth floor. Ignore friction. One person pushes to the right with a force of 50 N. The other pushes to the left with a force of 30 N.

The net force on the box is {{0}} toward the {{1}}. Using F = ma, the box's acceleration is {{2}}.

why: You added the forces, as if both people pushed the same way. They push in opposite directions, so subtract: 50 − 30.
30 N is just the left push. The net force combines both pushes: 50 N right minus 30 N left.
50 N is just the right push. The 30-N push to the left works against it, so subtract.

options: neither side, because the forces are balanced
why: The net force points toward the larger force. The right push (50 N) is larger than the left push (30 N).
The forces are not equal (50 N and 30 N), so they do not balance. There is a 20-N net force.
8 m/s<sup>2</sup> comes from using 80 N, the sum of the forces. Use the net force, 20 N: 20 ÷ 10 = 2.
You divided mass by force (10 ÷ 20). Acceleration is force divided by mass: a = F ÷ m = 20 ÷ 10.
You multiplied force by mass (20 × 10). That would be the force formula; for acceleration, divide: a = F ÷ m.

items.hint: The forces point in opposite directions, so subtract. Then use a = F ÷ m.
items.explain:
The forces are in opposite directions, so subtract: 50 N − 30 N = 20 N. The net force points toward the larger force, to the right.

a = F ÷ m = 20 N ÷ 10 kg = 2 m/s2.

Adding the forces (80 N) treats them as if both pushed the same way. 0.5 m/s2 comes from dividing mass by force (10 ÷ 20), and 200 m/s2 comes from multiplying (20 × 10).

items.prompt: A warehouse worker lifts a box that weighs 200 N straight up onto a shelf 1.5 m high. The lift takes 3 seconds. Work is calculated using W = Fd, and power is calculated using P = W/t. What is the worker's power output while lifting the box?
why: 300 is the work in joules (200 × 1.5). You skipped the second step: divide the work by the 3 seconds.
You multiplied the work by the time (300 × 3). Power is work divided by time.
You divided the force by the time (200 ÷ 3) and skipped the distance. Find the work first: 200 N × 1.5 m = 300 J.
items.hint: Find the work first, then divide by the time.
items.explain:
Step 1, work: W = F × d = 200 N × 1.5 m = 300 J.

Step 2, power: P = W ÷ t = 300 J ÷ 3 s = 100 W.

300 W is the work (300 J) with the time step skipped. 900 W comes from multiplying by the time instead of dividing (300 × 3). 67 W leaves out the distance (200 ÷ 3).

items.prompt: A hammer drives a nail into a board. While they are in contact, the hammer pushes on the nail with a force of 500 N. What force does the nail exert on the hammer?
options: 500 N, pointing back toward the hammer
Less than 500 N, because the nail moves into the board
More than 500 N, because the hammer stops after the hit
500 N, pointing the same way the hammer moves
why: Moving does not shrink the force pair. By the third law, the nail pushes back on the hammer just as hard as the hammer pushes on the nail.
The hammer stopping is an effect of the nail's push, not a sign of a bigger force. Third-law forces are always equal in size.
The size is right, but third-law forces point in opposite directions. The nail pushes back against the hammer.
items.hint: Newton's third law: equal size, opposite direction.
items.explain: By Newton's third law, the nail pushes on the hammer with a force equal in size (500 N) and opposite in direction, back toward the hammer. That backward push is what stops the hammer. The nail moves into the board and the hammer stops, but those different results come from the different objects and other forces involved, not from unequal force pairs.

items.prompt: Newton's second law states that F = ma. What was the net force on the 1,200-kg car from 0 seconds to 6 seconds?
why: You divided the mass by the acceleration (1,200 ÷ 3). Newton's second law multiplies them: F = m × a.
You multiplied the mass by the speed (1,200 × 18). F = ma needs the acceleration, 3 m/s<sup>2</sup>, not the speed.
0 N is the net force from 6 to 10 s, when the speed is constant. From 0 to 6 s the car speeds up, so the net force is not zero.
items.hint: First find the acceleration from the graph. Then multiply by the mass.
items.explain:
Step 1, acceleration: a = (18 m/s − 0 m/s) ÷ 6 s = 3 m/s2.

Step 2, net force: F = m × a = 1,200 kg × 3 m/s2 = 3,600 N.

400 N comes from dividing the mass by the acceleration (1,200 ÷ 3). 21,600 N uses the speed (18 m/s) instead of the acceleration. 0 N would be correct only for 6 to 10 s, when the speed is constant and the forces on the car are balanced.

items.prompt: A mover needs to raise a crate that weighs 600 N onto a platform 1.0 m high. Instead of lifting it straight up, he pushes it up a ramp that is 4.0 m long. Assuming there is no friction, the work done pushing the crate up the ramp equals the work needed to lift it straight up. What force must the mover apply along the ramp?
why: 600 N is the force to lift the crate straight up. The ramp spreads the same work over 4.0 m, so the force is smaller.
You multiplied the weight by the ramp length (600 × 4.0). A ramp reduces the force: divide the work by the length.
300 N assumes the ramp halves the force, like a movable pulley. This ramp's MA is length ÷ height = 4.0 ÷ 1.0 = 4.
items.hint: Work to lift straight up = 600 N × 1.0 m. The same work is done over 4.0 m along the ramp.
items.explain:
Work to lift straight up: W = F × d = 600 N × 1.0 m = 600 J.

The same 600 J is done along the 4.0-m ramp: F × 4.0 m = 600 J, so F = 600 ÷ 4.0 = 150 N.

The ramp's mechanical advantage is 600 N ÷ 150 N = 4 (also 4.0 m ÷ 1.0 m = 4). 600 N ignores the ramp's advantage. 2,400 N multiplies instead of divides; a ramp reduces the force needed, at the cost of a longer distance.

items.prompt: Which two objects in the table have greater momentum than the soccer ball? Select two answers.
why: The baseball is the fastest object, but its mass is tiny: 0.15 × 40 = 6 kg·m/s, which is less than the soccer ball's 8.
The bicycle has a large mass, but it is parked: 15 × 0 = 0 kg·m/s. An object that is not moving has no momentum.
items.hint: Find p = m × v for the soccer ball first, then for each choice.
items.explain:
Soccer ball: p = 0.40 × 20 = 8 kg·m/s.

  • Bowling ball: 6.0 × 2.0 = 12 kg·m/s (greater)
  • Toy wagon: 20 × 0.50 = 10 kg·m/s (greater)
  • Baseball: 0.15 × 40 = 6 kg·m/s (less)
  • Parked bicycle: 15 × 0 = 0 kg·m/s (less)

The baseball is the fastest object, and the bicycle has a large mass, but momentum depends on both mass and velocity. An object that is not moving has no momentum.

items.prompt: On a frictionless track, a 2.0-kg cart moving to the right at 3.0 m/s collides with a 1.0-kg cart that is at rest. The two carts lock together and move off as one unit. Total momentum is conserved in the collision. What is the speed of the joined carts just after the collision?
why: 3.0 m/s ignores the second cart's mass. The same 6.0 kg·m/s is now shared by 3.0 kg, so the speed must drop.
You averaged the two carts' speeds ((3.0 + 0) ÷ 2). Momentum depends on mass: divide the total momentum, 6.0, by the total mass, 3.0 kg.
6.0 is the total momentum in kg·m/s, not a speed. Divide it by the combined mass, 3.0 kg.
items.hint: Total momentum before = total momentum after. After the collision, the moving mass is 2.0 kg + 1.0 kg.
items.explain:
Momentum before: (2.0 kg × 3.0 m/s) + (1.0 kg × 0 m/s) = 6.0 kg·m/s.

Mass after: 2.0 kg + 1.0 kg = 3.0 kg.

Speed after: v = p ÷ m = 6.0 ÷ 3.0 = 2.0 m/s to the right.

3.0 m/s ignores the added mass of the second cart; the same momentum shared by more mass means a lower speed. 6.0 m/s is the total momentum, not a speed. 1.5 m/s simply averages the two speeds, which ignores the masses.

items.prompt: A mechanic uses a 1.2-m steel bar as a lever to lift one corner of an engine. That corner pushes down on the bar with 1,500 N. The fulcrum is placed 0.2 m from the engine, and the mechanic pushes down on the other end of the bar. For a lever, ideal mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load arm. Ignoring friction, what effort force, in newtons, must the mechanic apply?

mistakes.why: You used the whole bar, 1.2 m, as the effort arm (MA = 6). The effort arm runs from the fulcrum to the mechanic's end: 1.2 − 0.2 = 1.0 m, so MA = 5.
You multiplied the load by the MA. A lever with MA = 5 reduces the force: 1,500 ÷ 5.
1,500 N is the load. The lever's mechanical advantage lets the mechanic push with less force: 1,500 ÷ 5.

items.hint: The effort arm is the bar length minus the load arm. Then effort = load ÷ MA.
items.explain:
Load arm = 0.2 m. Effort arm = 1.2 m − 0.2 m = 1.0 m.

MA = effort arm ÷ load arm = 1.0 ÷ 0.2 = 5.

Effort force = load ÷ MA = 1,500 N ÷ 5 = 300 N.

The tempting error is to use the full 1.2-m bar as the effort arm, which gives MA = 6 and 250 N. The effort arm is measured from the fulcrum, not from the end of the bar.

items.prompt: A race car drives around a circular track at a steady 160 km/h. Which statement is true?
options: Its speed stays the same, but its velocity keeps changing.
Its velocity stays the same, because its speed does not change.
Its speed keeps changing, because the car is always turning.
It has no acceleration, because its speed stays at 160 km/h.
why: A steady speed is not a steady velocity. Velocity includes direction, and the car's direction changes all the way around the circle.
Turning changes direction, not speed. The car covers distance at a steady 160 km/h; only its direction changes.
Changing direction is acceleration, even at a steady speed. Because the velocity changes, the car is accelerating.
items.hint: Velocity = speed + direction. What happens to the direction on a circular track?
items.explain: The speed stays at 160 km/h, so the speed is constant. On a circle the direction changes every moment, so the velocity keeps changing. A changing velocity is acceleration, which is why the claim of no acceleration is also wrong.

items.prompt: During which time interval was the bus stopped to pick up students?
why: From 0 to 10 minutes the distance rises from 0 to 4 km, so the bus is moving. A stop shows as a flat line.
From 20 to 30 minutes the distance rises from 4 km to 10 km. That is the fastest part of the trip.
From 5 to 10 minutes the bus is still moving (2 km to 4 km). It stops only once the line goes flat at 10 minutes.
items.hint: On a distance-time graph, a stop looks like a flat line.
items.explain: The line is flat at 4 km from 10 to 20 minutes, so the bus's distance from the garage did not change: it was stopped. In every other interval listed, at least part of the line rises, which means the bus was moving.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the car's motion from 0 seconds to 4 seconds?
options: The car moves at a constant speed of 16 m/s.
The car is stopped, because the line on the graph is flat.
The car is speeding up by 16 m/s every second.
The car is slowing down at a steady rate.
why: A flat line means stopped only on a distance-time graph. This y-axis shows speed, and the speed is 16 m/s, not 0.
16 m/s is the speed itself, not a change per second. The flat line means the speed is not changing at all.
The car slows down only after 4 s, where the line slopes down. From 0 to 4 s the line is level.
items.hint: Read the y-axis label first. What does a flat line mean on this kind of graph?
items.explain: This is a speed-time graph. From 0 to 4 s, the line is flat at 16 m/s, so the car moves at a constant speed of 16 m/s. The braking begins at 4 s, where the line starts to slope down. Calling the flat part "stopped" reads the graph as if it showed distance.

items.prompt: During which part of the trip was the bus moving fastest?
options: It moved at the same speed whenever it was moving.
why: From 0 to 10 minutes the bus went 4 km in 10 min (0.4 km/min). From 20 to 30 minutes it went 6 km in 10 min, which is faster.
From 10 to 20 minutes the line is flat; the bus was stopped, so its speed was 0.
The two moving parts have different slopes: 0.4 km/min and 0.6 km/min. The later part of the line is steeper.
items.hint: Compare how steep the moving parts of the line are, or calculate distance ÷ time for each.
items.explain:
Speed for each moving part:

  • 0 to 10 min: 4 km ÷ 10 min = 0.4 km/min
  • 20 to 30 min: (10 − 4) km ÷ 10 min = 0.6 km/min

The bus was fastest from 20 to 30 minutes, where the line is steepest. From 10 to 20 minutes it was stopped.

items.prompt: What was the bus's average speed, in kilometers per hour, for the entire 30-minute trip, including the stop?

mistakes.why: You left out the 10-minute stop (10 km ÷ 20 min = 30 km/h). The question asks about the entire trip, so use all 30 minutes.
10 ÷ 30 ≈ 0.33 is in km per minute. Convert 30 minutes to 0.5 hour, then divide.
You multiplied 10 km by 0.5 h. Average speed is distance divided by time: 10 ÷ 0.5.

items.hint: Total distance ÷ total time. Change 30 minutes into hours first.
items.explain:
Total distance = 10 km. Total time = 30 min = 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 h.

Average speed = 10 km ÷ 0.5 h = 20 km/h.

Leaving out the stop gives 30 km/h, but the stop is part of the trip. Dividing 10 by 30 gives km per minute, not km/h.

items.prompt: Acceleration is calculated using the formula a = (final speed − starting speed) ÷ time. What was the car's acceleration from 4 seconds to 12 seconds, in m/s2? (A negative value means the car is slowing down.)

mistakes.why: The size is right, but the car is slowing down: final minus starting is 0 − 16 = −16, so the acceleration is negative.
You divided by 12, the clock reading at the end. The braking lasted from 4 s to 12 s, which is 8 seconds: −16 ÷ 8.
−16 m/s is the change in speed. Divide it by the 8 seconds of braking: −16 ÷ 8 = −2 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

items.hint: Read the speed at 4 s and at 12 s. The time is the length of the interval, not the clock reading.
items.explain:
At 4 s the speed is 16 m/s; at 12 s it is 0 m/s. The time interval is 12 − 4 = 8 s.

a = (0 − 16) ÷ 8 = −16 ÷ 8 = −2 m/s2.

Check with the graph: the speed drops by 4 m/s every 2 s, or 2 m/s each second. The negative sign shows the car is slowing down.

items.prompt: Drag each example into the box for the law of motion it best illustrates.
choices: A soccer ball sits still on the field until a player kicks it.
When a car turns sharply, a phone on the dashboard slides toward the outside of the turn.
A loaded wheelbarrow needs a bigger push than an empty one to speed up at the same rate.
A harder throw gives the same baseball a greater acceleration.
As water sprays forward from a fire hose, the hose pushes backward on the firefighter.
A walker pushes backward on the ground, and the ground pushes the walker forward.
items.why: The phone on the dashboard is the example most often misplaced. No force throws it outward; it keeps going straight (inertia) while the car turns beneath it, so it belongs with the first law.
items.hint: Is the object continuing what it was doing? Is force compared with mass and acceleration? Or are two objects pushing on each other?
items.explain:
First law (inertia): The ball stays at rest until a force acts. The phone keeps moving in a straight line while the car turns, so it slides toward the outside of the turn.

Second law (F = ma): The loaded wheelbarrow has more mass, so it needs more force for the same acceleration. A harder throw is a bigger force on the same mass, so the acceleration is greater.

Third law: The hose pushes water forward and the water pushes the hose back; the walker pushes the ground back and the ground pushes the walker forward. Each is a pair of equal, opposite forces on two objects.

items.prompt:
Tasha pulls a 15-kg wagon forward with a force of 75 N. Friction acts on the wagon in the backward direction with a force of 30 N.

The net force on the wagon is {{0}} in the {{1}} direction. Using F = ma, the wagon's acceleration is {{2}}.

why: You added the forces. Friction points backward, against the pull, so subtract it: 75 − 30.
30 N is only the friction force. The net force combines the pull and friction: 75 − 30.
75 N is only Tasha's pull. Friction works against it, so subtract the 30 N.

options: neither direction, because the forces are balanced
why: The net force points toward the larger force. Tasha's 75-N pull forward is larger than the 30-N friction backward.
The forces are 75 N and 30 N, which are not equal, so they do not balance. There is a 45-N net force.
7 m/s<sup>2</sup> comes from 105 N, the sum of the forces. Use the net force: 45 ÷ 15 = 3.
You divided mass by force (15 ÷ 45). Acceleration is force divided by mass: 45 ÷ 15.
You multiplied the net force by the mass (45 × 15). For acceleration, divide: a = F ÷ m.

items.hint: Friction acts against the pull, so subtract. Then divide the net force by the mass.
items.explain:
Net force: 75 N forward − 30 N backward = 45 N, pointing forward (toward the larger force).

a = F ÷ m = 45 N ÷ 15 kg = 3 m/s2.

Using 105 N (adding the forces) gives 7 m/s2, but friction works against the pull. Dividing 15 by 45 or multiplying 45 by 15 uses the formula backward.

items.prompt: A crane lifts a 2,000-N steel beam straight up 15 m in 20 seconds. Work is calculated using W = Fd, and power is calculated using P = W/t. What is the crane's power output while lifting the beam?
why: 30,000 is the work in joules (2,000 × 15). You skipped the second step: divide the work by the 20 seconds.
You multiplied the work by the time (30,000 × 20). Power is work divided by time.
You divided the force by the time (2,000 ÷ 20) and skipped the distance. Find the work first: 2,000 N × 15 m = 30,000 J.
items.hint: Find the work first, then divide by the time.
items.explain:
Step 1, work: W = F × d = 2,000 N × 15 m = 30,000 J.

Step 2, power: P = W ÷ t = 30,000 J ÷ 20 s = 1,500 W.

30,000 W stops after the work step. 600,000 W multiplies by the time instead of dividing. 100 W leaves out the 15-m distance.

items.prompt: A woman jumps straight up. While her feet are pushing off, they push down on the ground with a force of 900 N. What force does the ground exert on her feet?
options: Less than 900 N, because she leaves the ground
More than 900 N, because the ground is so massive
why: Leaving the ground does not make the force pair unequal. By the third law, the ground pushes up on her exactly as hard as she pushes down on it.
The ground's huge mass affects how much the ground accelerates (almost not at all), not the size of the force. Third-law forces are equal.
The size is right, but the reaction force points the opposite way. She pushes down, so the ground pushes up; that upward push launches her.
items.hint: Newton's third law: the push back is equal in size and opposite in direction.
items.explain: By Newton's third law, the ground pushes on her feet with a force equal in size (900 N) and opposite in direction (upward). That upward push is what launches her into the air. The ground barely moves because its mass is enormous (second law), but the forces themselves are equal.

items.prompt: Newton's second law states that F = ma. What is the size of the net force on the 1,500-kg car while it is braking, from 4 seconds to 12 seconds?
why: You divided the mass by the acceleration (1,500 ÷ 2). Newton's second law multiplies them: F = m × a.
You multiplied the mass by the starting speed (1,500 × 16). F = ma needs the acceleration, 2 m/s<sup>2</sup>, not the speed.
0 N is the net force from 0 to 4 s, when the speed is constant. During braking the speed changes, so the net force is not zero.
items.hint: Find the size of the acceleration during braking first, then multiply by the mass.
items.explain:
Step 1, acceleration: a = (0 − 16) ÷ (12 − 4) = −16 ÷ 8 = −2 m/s2. Its size is 2 m/s2.

Step 2, net force: F = m × a = 1,500 kg × 2 m/s2 = 3,000 N, pointing backward, opposite the car's motion.

750 N divides instead of multiplies, 24,000 N uses the speed instead of the acceleration, and 0 N describes only the constant-speed part before braking.

items.prompt: A wheelchair ramp is 6.0 m long and rises 0.50 m to a doorway. A person and wheelchair weigh 900 N together. Assuming there is no friction, the work done moving up the ramp equals the work needed to lift the person and chair straight up. What force along the ramp is needed?
why: 900 N is the force to lift straight up. The long ramp spreads the work over 6.0 m, so much less force is needed.
You multiplied the weight by the ramp length (900 × 6.0). A ramp reduces the force: divide the work by the length.
450 is the work in joules (900 × 0.50), not the force. You still need to spread that work over the 6.0-m ramp: 450 ÷ 6.0.
items.hint: Work to lift straight up = weight × height. Spread that same work over the ramp length.
items.explain:
Work to lift straight up: 900 N × 0.50 m = 450 J.

Along the ramp: F × 6.0 m = 450 J, so F = 450 ÷ 6.0 = 75 N.

Check with MA: 6.0 m ÷ 0.50 m = 12, and 900 N ÷ 12 = 75 N. Stopping at 450 gives the work, not the force.

items.prompt: Which two objects in the table have greater momentum than the jogger? Select two answers.
why: The football is the fastest object, but its mass is tiny: 0.40 × 25 = 10 kg·m/s, far less than the jogger's 150.
The child moves as fast as the cyclist, but has much less mass: 30 × 4.0 = 120 kg·m/s, which is less than 150.
The motor scooter is heavy, but parked: 100 × 0 = 0 kg·m/s. No motion means no momentum.
items.hint: Find the jogger's momentum first (60 × 2.5), then compare each choice.
items.explain:
Jogger: p = 60 × 2.5 = 150 kg·m/s.

  • Cyclist with bike: 75 × 4.0 = 300 kg·m/s (greater)
  • Golf cart: 400 × 0.50 = 200 kg·m/s (greater)
  • Child on a scooter: 30 × 4.0 = 120 kg·m/s (less)
  • Thrown football: 0.40 × 25 = 10 kg·m/s (less)
  • Parked motor scooter: 100 × 0 = 0 kg·m/s (less)

The slow golf cart beats the jogger because of its large mass; the fast football does not, because its mass is so small.

items.prompt: A 1,200-kg car moving at 15 m/s rear-ends an 800-kg car that is stopped at a light. The two cars lock together. Assume total momentum is conserved. What is the speed of the joined cars just after the collision?
why: 15 m/s ignores the second car's mass. The same momentum is now shared by 2,000 kg, so the speed must drop.
You averaged the two speeds ((15 + 0) ÷ 2). Momentum depends on mass: divide the total momentum by the total mass.
You divided the momentum by only the stopped car's mass (18,000 ÷ 800). After the crash both cars move together, so divide by 2,000 kg.
items.hint: Momentum before = 1,200 × 15. After the crash, the moving mass is 1,200 + 800.
items.explain:
Momentum before: (1,200 × 15) + (800 × 0) = 18,000 kg·m/s.

Mass after: 1,200 + 800 = 2,000 kg.

v = 18,000 ÷ 2,000 = 9 m/s.

The joined cars must move slower than 15 m/s, because the same momentum is spread over more mass. Averaging the speeds (7.5 m/s) ignores the masses.

items.prompt: A worker uses a 2.0-m pry bar as a lever to raise the edge of a heavy crate. The crate pushes down on the bar with 1,600 N. The fulcrum is placed 0.4 m from the crate, and the worker pushes down on the other end of the bar. For a lever, ideal mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load arm. Ignoring friction, what effort force, in newtons, must the worker apply?

mistakes.why: You used the whole bar, 2.0 m, as the effort arm (MA = 5). The effort arm runs from the fulcrum to the worker's end: 2.0 − 0.4 = 1.6 m, so MA = 4.
You multiplied the load by the MA. A lever with MA = 4 reduces the force: 1,600 ÷ 4.
1,600 N is the load. The lever's mechanical advantage lets the worker push with less force: 1,600 ÷ 4.

items.hint: The effort arm is the bar length minus the load arm. Then effort = load ÷ MA.
items.explain:
Load arm = 0.4 m. Effort arm = 2.0 m − 0.4 m = 1.6 m.

MA = 1.6 ÷ 0.4 = 4.

Effort force = 1,600 N ÷ 4 = 400 N.

Using the full 2.0-m bar as the effort arm gives MA = 5 and 320 N, but the effort arm is measured from the fulcrum.

items.prompt: Acceleration is calculated using a = (final speed − starting speed) ÷ time. What was the drone's acceleration from 0 to 20 seconds, in m/s2?

mistakes.why: 1.2 comes from 12 ÷ 10, but the drone took 20 seconds, not 10, to reach 12 m/s. Divide 12 by 20.
12 m/s is the change in speed. Divide it by the 20 seconds it took: 12 ÷ 20 = 0.6 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
You divided by 60 s, the whole flight. The drone sped up only from 0 to 20 s, so divide by 20.

items.explain:
At 0 s the speed is 0 m/s; at 20 s it is 12 m/s.

a = (12 − 0) ÷ 20 = 0.6 m/s2.

Check: the speed rises 6 m/s every 10 s, which is 0.6 m/s each second.

items.prompt: Distance = speed × time. How far did the drone travel from 20 seconds to 40 seconds?
why: The flat line does not mean the drone stopped. This is a speed-time graph: the drone moved at a constant 12 m/s for those 20 seconds.
12 m/s is the speed, not a distance. Multiply the speed by the 20 seconds of travel.
You multiplied by 40, the clock reading at the end. The interval lasted 40 − 20 = 20 seconds.
items.explain:
The y-axis shows speed. From 20 to 40 s the line is flat at 12 m/s, so the drone flies at a constant 12 m/s for 20 s.

d = s × t = 12 m/s × 20 s = 240 m.

The tempting answer 0 m reads the flat line as "stopped," which is only true on a distance-time graph.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the students' data?
options: With the same net force, doubling the cart's mass cut its acceleration in half.
Adding mass to the cart caused the cart's acceleration to increase.
An 8.0-kg cart pulled with this force would have no acceleration at all.
A cart's acceleration does not depend on the size of the net force on it.
why: This reverses the pattern. As the mass went from 1.0 kg to 4.0 kg, the acceleration fell from 6.0 to 1.5 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
8.0 kg was not tested, and F = ma predicts 6.0 ÷ 8.0 = 0.75 m/s<sup>2</sup>, not zero. Any net force gives some acceleration.
The force was held at 6.0 N in every trial, so this experiment cannot show anything about changing the force. The claim goes beyond the data.
items.explain:
Compare pairs where the mass doubles: 1.0 kg → 2.0 kg, acceleration 6.0 → 3.0 m/s2; 2.0 kg → 4.0 kg, acceleration 3.0 → 1.5 m/s2. Each time the mass doubled, the acceleration was cut in half, just as a = F ÷ m predicts.

The claim about force goes beyond the data, because force was a controlled variable. The 8.0-kg claim extrapolates and contradicts F = ma.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements about the cart experiment.

The independent variable is {{0}}, and the dependent variable is {{1}}. For the 2.0-kg cart, F = m × a gives a net force of {{2}}, which matches the force the students used.

options: the net force on the cart
why: Acceleration is what the motion sensor measured, so it is the dependent variable.
The net force was kept at 6.0 N in every trial, so it is a controlled variable, not the one being changed.
The same smooth table was used in every trial, so it is a controlled condition.

options: the net force on the cart
the reading on the spring scale
why: The students changed the mass on purpose by adding blocks, so mass is the independent variable.
The net force stayed at 6.0 N, so it is a controlled variable. The dependent variable is what was measured as a result.
The spring scale was used to keep the force at 6.0 N; its reading was held constant, not measured as a result.
You divided acceleration by mass (3.0 ÷ 2.0). F = m × a, so multiply: 2.0 × 3.0.
You divided mass by acceleration (2.0 ÷ 3.0). F = m × a, so multiply.
You added the mass and acceleration (2.0 + 3.0). F = m × a means multiply: 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 N.

items.explain:
The students changed the mass on purpose, so it is the independent variable. They measured the acceleration, so it is the dependent variable. The net force (6.0 N) was controlled.

For the 2.0-kg cart: F = 2.0 kg × 3.0 m/s2 = 6.0 N, matching the force used, which supports Newton's second law.

items.prompt: In a crash test, a car moving at 50 km/h hits a wall and stops suddenly. A crash-test dummy without a seat belt keeps moving forward and hits the dashboard. Which statement best explains the dummy's motion?
options: First law: the dummy keeps moving forward until a force stops it.
Second law: the car's large mass gives the dummy a forward acceleration.
Third law: the car pushes the dummy forward as the dummy pushes the car.
First law: the crash creates a forward force that throws the dummy ahead.
why: Nothing pushes the dummy forward, so there is no forward acceleration from the car. The dummy simply keeps the motion it already had.
Once the car stops, it is not pushing the dummy forward at all. The dummy continues forward on its own because of inertia.
The right law, but the wrong reason. No forward force acts on the dummy; it keeps moving because nothing has stopped it yet.
items.explain: This is Newton's first law (inertia). The dummy was moving at 50 km/h along with the car. When the wall stops the car, nothing stops the dummy, so it keeps moving forward until the dashboard (or a seat belt) pushes on it. No forward force is needed to keep it moving, which is why the "forward force" explanation is wrong even though it names the first law.

items.prompt: Ray and Lee each lift an identical 300-N box straight up onto a platform 1.2 m high. Ray takes 2 s, and Lee takes 4 s. Use W = Fd and P = W/t. Which statement is correct?
options: Both do 360 J of work; Ray's power is 180 W and Lee's is 90 W.
Ray does twice as much work as Lee, because Ray lifts twice as fast.
Both use 360 W of power, because they do exactly the same work.
Lee does more work and uses more power, because he lifts for longer.
why: Work does not depend on time. Both lift 300 N through 1.2 m, so both do 360 J. Lifting faster raises the power, not the work.
360 is the work in joules, not the power. Power divides work by time, so the two workers, with different times, have different powers.
More time does not mean more work; both do 360 J. Taking longer actually means less power: 360 ÷ 4 = 90 W.
items.explain:
Work: W = 300 N × 1.2 m = 360 J for both workers. Time is not part of work.

Power: Ray, 360 ÷ 2 = 180 W; Lee, 360 ÷ 4 = 90 W.

The same work done in half the time takes twice the power. Saying Ray does more work confuses work with power.

items.prompt: A worker pushes a 500-N box up a 5-m ramp onto a platform 1 m high instead of lifting it straight up. Ignore friction. Which two statements are true? Select two answers.
options: The push needed along the ramp is 100 N.
The work done is 500 J either way.
The ramp cuts the work needed down to 100 J.
The box moves a shorter distance on the ramp than when lifted.
why: A ramp reduces the force, not the work. 100 N × 5 m = 500 J, the same as lifting 500 N × 1 m.
It is the other way around: the box travels 5 m along the ramp instead of 1 m straight up. That longer distance is the price of the smaller force.
You divided height by length (1 ÷ 5). The ideal MA of a ramp is length ÷ height = 5 ÷ 1 = 5.
items.explain:
Work to lift straight up: 500 N × 1 m = 500 J. An ideal ramp needs the same work, so F × 5 m = 500 J and F = 100 N. The ramp's MA is 5 ÷ 1 = 5 (or 500 N ÷ 100 N).

The ramp trades less force for more distance (5 m instead of 1 m). It never reduces the work.

items.prompt: A 60-kg ice skater gliding at 4 m/s grabs a 20-kg child who is standing still on the ice. They glide off together. Total momentum is conserved. What is their speed just after the skater grabs the child, in m/s?

mistakes.why: 4 m/s ignores the child's mass. The same 240 kg·m/s is now shared by 80 kg, so the speed drops: 240 ÷ 80.
You averaged the two speeds ((4 + 0) ÷ 2). Divide the total momentum, 240 kg·m/s, by the total mass, 80 kg.
You divided the momentum by only the child's mass (240 ÷ 20). They move together, so divide by 60 + 20 = 80 kg.

items.explain:
Momentum before: (60 × 4) + (20 × 0) = 240 kg·m/s.

Mass after: 60 + 20 = 80 kg.

v = 240 ÷ 80 = 3 m/s. It must be less than 4 m/s, because the same momentum is shared by more mass.

items.prompt: Acceleration is calculated using a = (final speed − starting speed) ÷ time. What was the train's acceleration from 0 to 30 seconds, in m/s2?

mistakes.why: 1.5 comes from 15 ÷ 10, but the train took 30 seconds, not 10, to reach 15 m/s. Divide 15 by 30.
15 m/s is the change in speed. Divide it by the 30 seconds it took: 15 ÷ 30 = 0.5 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
You divided by 60 s, the whole minute. The train sped up only from 0 to 30 s, so divide by 30.

items.explain:
At 0 s the speed is 0 m/s; at 30 s it is 15 m/s.

a = (15 − 0) ÷ 30 = 0.5 m/s2.

Check: the speed rises 5 m/s every 10 s, which is 0.5 m/s each second.

items.prompt: Distance = speed × time. How far did the train travel from 30 seconds to 60 seconds?
why: The flat line does not mean the train stopped. This is a speed-time graph: the train moved at a constant 15 m/s for those 30 seconds.
15 m/s is the speed, not a distance. Multiply the speed by the 30 seconds of travel.
You multiplied by 60, the clock reading at the end. The interval lasted 60 − 30 = 30 seconds.
items.explain:
The y-axis shows speed. From 30 to 60 s the line is flat at 15 m/s, so the train moves at a constant 15 m/s for 30 s.

d = s × t = 15 m/s × 30 s = 450 m.

The tempting answer 0 m reads the flat line as "stopped," which is only true on a distance-time graph.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the students' data?
options: With the mass held constant, doubling the net force doubled the acceleration.
Increasing the net force on the cart caused its acceleration to decrease.
The acceleration rose by 2.0 m/s<sup>2</sup> for each 2.0-N increase in force.
The mass of a cart has no effect on how quickly the cart accelerates.
why: This reverses the pattern. As the force rose from 2.0 N to 8.0 N, the acceleration rose from 1.0 to 4.0 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
Read the table again: each 2.0-N increase raised the acceleration by only 1.0 m/s<sup>2</sup> (1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0).
The mass was held at 2.0 kg in every trial, so this experiment cannot show anything about changing the mass. The claim goes beyond the data.
items.explain:
Compare pairs where the force doubles: 2.0 N → 4.0 N, acceleration 1.0 → 2.0 m/s2; 4.0 N → 8.0 N, acceleration 2.0 → 4.0 m/s2. Each time the force doubled, the acceleration doubled, just as a = F ÷ m predicts.

The claim about mass goes beyond the data, because mass was a controlled variable. The "2.0 m/s2 per 2.0 N" claim misreads the table.

Complete the statements about the cart experiment.

The independent variable is {{0}}, and the dependent variable is {{1}}. For the 6.0-N trial, rearranging F = m × a gives a mass of {{2}}, which matches the cart's actual mass.

options: the net force on the cart

The cart's mass stayed at 2.0 kg in every trial, so it is a controlled variable.
The same smooth table was used in every trial, so it is a controlled condition.

options: the net force on the cart
the reading on the spring scale

The mass stayed at 2.0 kg, so it is a controlled variable. The dependent variable is what was measured as a result.

You multiplied force by acceleration (6.0 × 3.0). Mass = F ÷ a.
You divided acceleration by force (3.0 ÷ 6.0). Mass = F ÷ a = 6.0 ÷ 3.0.

items.explain:
The students changed the net force on purpose, so it is the independent variable. They measured the acceleration, so it is the dependent variable. The mass (2.0 kg) was controlled.

For the 6.0-N trial: m = F ÷ a = 6.0 N ÷ 3.0 m/s2 = 2.0 kg, matching the cart's mass, which supports Newton's second law.

items.prompt: An astronaut floating at rest outside a space station throws a wrench forward. As the wrench flies away, she drifts backward. Which statement best explains her motion?
options: Third law: she pushes the wrench forward, so the wrench pushes her back.
First law: her body keeps moving backward because nothing stops it.
Second law: the wrench has less mass, so it pulls her backward with it.
Third law: her push on the wrench is larger than its push back on her.
why: She was at rest before the throw, so inertia cannot explain why she starts moving backward. A force had to act on her: the wrench's push.
The wrench does not pull her; it moves away from her. Her backward motion comes from the wrench pushing back on her hand.
The right law, but the wrong reason. Third-law forces are always equal in size; she moves more slowly than the wrench because her mass is larger.
items.explain: This is Newton's third law. Her hand pushes the wrench forward, and the wrench pushes her hand backward with an equal and opposite force. The wrench flies off fast and she drifts back slowly because her mass is much larger (second law), not because the forces are unequal.

items.prompt: Two freight elevators each lift an identical 6,000-N load 10 m. Elevator 1 takes 15 s, and Elevator 2 takes 30 s. Use W = Fd and P = W/t. Which statement is correct?
options: Both do 60,000 J of work; Elevator 1 uses 4,000 W and Elevator 2 uses 2,000 W.
Elevator 1 does twice as much work, because it lifts the load twice as fast.
Both use 60,000 W of power, because they do exactly the same amount of work.
Elevator 2 does more work and uses more power, because it runs for longer.
why: Work does not depend on time. Both lift 6,000 N through 10 m, so both do 60,000 J. Lifting faster raises the power, not the work.
60,000 is the work in joules, not the power. Power divides work by time, so elevators with different times have different powers.
More time does not mean more work; both do 60,000 J. Taking longer means less power: 60,000 ÷ 30 = 2,000 W.
items.explain:
Work: W = 6,000 N × 10 m = 60,000 J for both elevators.

Power: Elevator 1, 60,000 ÷ 15 = 4,000 W; Elevator 2, 60,000 ÷ 30 = 2,000 W.

The same work done in half the time takes twice the power. Saying the faster elevator does more work confuses work with power.

items.prompt: A worker uses a 3.0-m steel bar as a lever to lift a 1,200-N rock. The fulcrum is 0.6 m from the rock, and she pushes down on the other end of the bar. Ignore friction. Which two statements are true? Select two answers.
options: The effort force she needs is 300 N.
Her end of the bar moves 4 times as far as the rock rises.
The lever cuts the work she must do to one-fourth.
why: A lever reduces the force, not the work. She pushes with one-fourth the force but over four times the distance, so the work is the same.
5 comes from using the whole 3.0-m bar as the effort arm. The effort arm runs from the fulcrum: 3.0 − 0.6 = 2.4 m, so MA = 2.4 ÷ 0.6 = 4.
You divided load arm by effort arm (0.6 ÷ 2.4). A lever's MA = effort arm ÷ load arm = 2.4 ÷ 0.6 = 4.
items.explain:
Load arm = 0.6 m; effort arm = 3.0 − 0.6 = 2.4 m. MA = 2.4 ÷ 0.6 = 4.

Effort = 1,200 N ÷ 4 = 300 N. Because work stays the same, her end must move 4 times as far as the rock rises (for example, 0.4 m to lift the rock 0.1 m: 300 × 0.4 = 1,200 × 0.1 = 120 J).

A lever never reduces the work, and measuring the effort arm from the end of the bar instead of the fulcrum gives the wrong MA of 5.

items.prompt: A 2,000-kg railroad car rolling at 6 m/s couples with (locks onto) a 1,000-kg car that is at rest. The two cars roll off together. Total momentum is conserved. What is their speed just after coupling, in m/s?

mistakes.why: 6 m/s ignores the second car's mass. The same 12,000 kg·m/s is now shared by 3,000 kg, so the speed drops: 12,000 ÷ 3,000.
You averaged the two speeds ((6 + 0) ÷ 2). Divide the total momentum, 12,000 kg·m/s, by the total mass, 3,000 kg.
You divided the momentum by only the resting car's mass (12,000 ÷ 1,000). They roll together, so divide by 3,000 kg.

items.explain:
Momentum before: (2,000 × 6) + (1,000 × 0) = 12,000 kg·m/s.

Mass after: 2,000 + 1,000 = 3,000 kg.

v = 12,000 ÷ 3,000 = 4 m/s. It must be less than 6 m/s, because the same momentum is shared by more mass.

vocab.def: How fast an object moves; distance divided by time.
vocab.example: A car that travels 120 miles in 2 hours has an average speed of 60 mi/h.
A plane flying 500 km/h due north.

vocab.def: The rate at which velocity changes: speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction. Measured in m/s<sup>2</sup>.
vocab.example: A runner who goes from 0 to 6 m/s in 2 s accelerates at 3 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

vocab.def: A push or a pull on an object, measured in newtons (N).
vocab.example: Friction, gravity, and a hand pushing a door are all forces.

vocab.def: The overall force on an object after all the forces acting on it are combined.
vocab.example: 30 N right and 10 N left give a net force of 20 N right.

vocab.def: Forces that combine to a net force of zero, so the object's motion does not change.
vocab.example: A lamp resting on a table: gravity down equals the table's push up.

vocab.def: The tendency of an object to resist a change in its motion; more mass means more inertia.
vocab.example: A loaded shopping cart is harder to start and stop than an empty one.

vocab.def: A force that acts against motion when two surfaces rub or slide past each other.
vocab.example: Friction between tires and the road lets a car stop.

vocab.def: The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg). It does not change from place to place.
vocab.example: A 70-kg person has a mass of 70 kg on Earth or on the Moon.

vocab.def: The force of gravity on an object; weight = mass × g, with g ≈ 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> on Earth.
vocab.example: A 10-kg bag weighs about 98 N on Earth.

vocab.def: Energy transferred when a force moves an object in the direction of the force; W = F × d, in joules (J).
vocab.example: Lifting a 50-N box 2 m does 100 J of work.

vocab.def: How fast work is done; P = W ÷ t, in watts (W).
vocab.example: Doing 600 J of work in 3 s is 200 W of power.

vocab.def: How many times a machine multiplies the input force; output force ÷ input force.
vocab.example: A ramp that lets 100 N of push move a 400-N box has an MA of 4.

vocab.def: Mass in motion; p = m × v, in kg·m/s. Total momentum is conserved in a collision.
vocab.example: A 0.5-kg ball moving at 8 m/s has a momentum of 4 kg·m/s.

vocab.def: The fixed point a lever turns on. Effort arm and load arm are measured from it.
vocab.example: On a seesaw, the fulcrum is the post in the middle.

Motion Graphs (read the y-axis first!)

  • Distance-time: flat = stopped; straight up-slope = constant speed; steeper = faster; slope = speed.
  • Speed-time: flat = constant speed; up-slope = speeding up; down-slope = slowing down; slope = acceleration.

Net Force

  • Same direction: add. Opposite: subtract (points toward the larger force).
  • Net 0 = balanced = no change in motion.
  • Net ≠ 0 = unbalanced = acceleration.

Newton's Laws

  1. Inertia: no net force, no change in motion.
  2. F = ma: more force, more acceleration; more mass, less acceleration.
  3. Action-reaction: equal and opposite forces on different objects.

Simple Machines

Lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, screw. Less force, more distance; work stays the same (ideal). Ramp MA = length ÷ height. Lever MA = effort arm ÷ load arm.

Momentum

Total p before = total p after (no outside forces).

Graph check: the time in a formula is the length of the interval (end − start), not the clock reading. Distance at constant speed = speed × time.
